## Description
abbrev: /FAIL`<CR>` searches for "/FAIL`<C-]><CR>`" (literal text, no search)

- source: lua/genja/abbreviations.vim:38, the cmdline `<CR>` map returns the single-quoted string `'<C-]><CR>'` for every cmdtype but `:`; in an `<expr>` map the <> is typed literally, and the Vim-only `<C-]>` is only needed for `:` abbreviations (a3e07a3, 80c8fa1)
- fix: only `:` gets the `<C-]>` prefix, other cmdtypes return `"\<CR>"` (double quotes, real key), or no map at all for `/` `?`
- test: `/FAIL<CR>`, `?FAIL<CR>`, `:s/a/b/<CR>`, `jj`, `g` still work
- 2026-11-02: fixed (abbreviations.vim: `"\<CR>"` for non-`:`); `/FAIL<CR>` tested by hand, the rest of the test list open (82cd9a4)

## Description
Merge a PR branch into base in git's object store, without a work tree: `git merge-tree --write-tree`,
`git commit-tree` with both parents, then `git update-ref` with the old value of base, so a base that
moved in the meantime is not overwritten.
The clean path is used when base is not the branch checked out in the main checkout. When base is
checked out, Merge works as today. Hooks on the merge commit do not matter (`commit-tree` runs none).
When base moved during the merge, nothing is saved and Ops offers to rebase head onto the new base,
then merge it. Rebase is the strong preference (decided 2026-11-15): the history of base stays one
straight line. The user confirms the offer; it does not run by itself. The
backend (`git.merge` in the relay, branch `PR-merge-action`) runs the commands.
Change: `openspec/changes/merge-beside-checkout/` (sections "A clean merge, without a work tree" and
"Main moved while I was deciding").
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] #1 merge-tree, commit-tree and update-ref with the old value, in `git.merge`
- [ ] #2 used only when base is not the branch checked out in the main checkout
- [ ] #3 base moved during the merge: nothing saved, Ops offers to rebase head onto the new base, then merge
- [ ] #4 `main` checked out in an agent's worktree: that worktree is left alone
## Verify
- [ ] manual: clean main checkout on base: Merge works as before
- [ ] manual: main checkout on another branch: merging into `main` leaves the branch, files and buffers alone
- [ ] manual: commit to `main` while the merge is running: no merge commit, the offer to merge again appears
- [ ] manual: accept the offer: head is rebased onto the new `main`, then merged; `main` history is linear

status: To Do
assignee: []
created_date: '2026-11-23'
labels:
- ops

dependencies: []
ordinal: 205000
## Description
ops: make the app safe on input it does not own. A repository is data plus prose plus a `.git`
directory, and today the app can execute from all three: the New change agent writes with
`acceptEdits` after reading repo prose, rendered markdown hands any URI scheme to Explorer, four call
sites start through `cmd /c start`, git reads hooks and exec-capable config, and the relay is an
unauthenticated TCP API that reaches `nvim_exec_lua`. The change defines the threat model, hardens
the git and shell doors, contains paths, makes the agent draft instead of write, and refuses a
non-loopback relay unless the user says so out loud. P1 findings (release signing, log retention,
PDF sandboxing, named pipe) are named follow-ups, not this task.
Change: `openspec/changes/ops-security-posture/`
## Acceptance Criteria
<!-- AC:BEGIN -->

- [ ] #1 a hostile fixture (exec-capable `.git/config`, a hook, six link shapes, a junction, `a & b`, an outside `.nvimos`) is opened, diffed and committed without running its code or touching outside the repo
- [ ] #2 rendered links: only `http`, `https` and `mailto` reach the shell; unknown schemes and UNC paths do not
- [ ] #3 no `cmd /c start` remains; a folder named `a & b` starts only the editor
- [ ] #4 the agent drafts read-only and the app writes only the change directory and its task file; `.git/**` is refused
- [ ] #5 `:NvimosServe 0.0.0.0:6666` refuses without `!`; the app will not store a remote address and says it is unencrypted
- [ ] #6 discard honours the trash setting; writes and deletes are contained by `resolveInside`
- [ ] #7 `SECURITY.md` and a Help Security group exist; `make test` and `flutter analyze` pass

## Description
In `~/es/nvimos-poc-frontend`, checking items feels slow: it takes a while before a checkbox
shows as checked. Measure where the time goes and fix both kinds of click:
- Tasks checklists (task detail, a change's Tasks tab, the review panel). `Workspace.edit` is
already optimistic, but each edit re-parses every planning file on the UI thread, and the file
write triggers a full reload (every planning file, branches, commits ahead); a reload that
started before the click can finish after it and show the old state for a moment.
- Changes stage checkboxes. Not optimistic: a click waits for the stage call, `git status` and
the file's diff before it redraws.
Add UI timing instrumentation: record every UI interaction per session, and write a state file
when the app quits. On during development, off in production. Hook it where clicks already
pass (backend wrapper, state actions, Flutter's global pointer route), not into click handlers.
## Original instructions
The user's words, 2026-11-11:
> So the app seems kind of slow when I check items and so on. It takes a while before they are
> checked. Can you do the classical UI trick where you change the UI right after the click? And
> then as the responses come in, you either reject the change or do nothing. I mean, if the
> change applied, so I'm coming from a web client server kind of perspective, before you do any
> radical changes to the Flutter app. Can you tell me if this is even possible? Or maybe I should

# Replacing nvim-cmp with blink.cmp in genja-completion011
Done 2026-10-27 (tag before-blink-2026-w44 is the state before). Checked against cmp.saghen.dev (blink.cmp v1.10.2).
## Upstream facts that matter here
- Install: `saghen/blink.cmp`, `version = '1.*'`: lazy checks out a release tag and blink downloads its prebuilt Rust fuzzy matcher (needs curl and git).
- Windows x86_64 has a prebuilt binary (`libblink_cmp_fuzzy.dll` in `nvim-data/lazy/blink.cmp/target/release/`).
- `fuzzy.implementation = 'prefer_rust_with_warning'` falls back to the Lua matcher when the binary is missing; `'lua'` needs no binary at all.
- Neovim 0.11: blink adds its LSP capabilities itself; `require('blink.cmp').get_lsp_capabilities()` is only needed to merge your own.
- Off per buffer: `vim.b.completion = false` (the default `enabled` also skips `buftype=prompt`).
- Per filetype: `sources.per_filetype = { lua = { inherit_defaults = true, 'lazydev' } }`.
- Providers: `score_offset`, `min_keyword_length`, `max_items`, `fallbacks` (used when a provider returns nothing), `enabled` (may be a function).
- Defaults: path `score_offset = 3`; buffer `-3`; `lsp` and `path` fall back to `buffer`.
- Custom source: a module with `new(opts)`, optional `enabled()` and `get_trigger_characters()`, and `get_completions(ctx, callback)`.
- `callback({ items, is_incomplete_forward, is_incomplete_backward })`.
- blink filters by keyword itself; the source must not.
- Kinds come from `require('blink.cmp.types').CompletionItemKind`.
- Registered under `sources.providers.<id> = { name, module, opts }`.
- Cmdline: on by default, preset `'cmdline'`: `<Tab>`/`<S-Tab>` show and select, `<C-n>`/`<C-p>`, `<C-y>` accept, `<C-e>` cancel. Menu `auto_show` is off by default.
- Selection defaults: `preselect = true`, `auto_insert = true`; with these, `<CR>` would accept the first item without a selection.
- Snippets: preset `default` uses `vim.snippet`; friendly-snippets only if installed.
## Feature by feature (lua/genja/completion/*.lua)
| file | today (nvim-cmp) | blink.cmp | work |
| init.lua | features fill one `cmp.setup()` table | features fill one blink `opts` table; `require('blink.cmp').setup(opts)` | small: the loop stays, the table shape changes |

| keymaps | `<Tab>` next/snippet/complete, `<S-Tab>`, `<CR>` confirm only a selected item, `<F2>`/`<F3>`, `^K` abort, `<C-Space>` | `keymap = { preset = 'none', ['<Tab>'] = { 'select_next', 'snippet_forward', <fn: show if text before>, 'fallback' }, ... }`; `<CR>` = `{ 'accept', 'fallback' }` with `completion.list.selection.preselect = false` | medium: the has-text-before check becomes a function command |
| snippets | `vim.snippet.expand` | built in (`snippets.preset = 'default'`) | delete the file |
| lsp | `nvim_lsp`, group 1 | built-in `lsp` | delete; `lsp/init.lua` drops the `cmp_nvim_lsp` capabilities block |
| path | `path`, group 1 | built-in `path` | delete |
| buffer | `buffer`, group 2 (only when lsp/path are empty) | built-in `buffer`; the default fallbacks already do "only when empty" | delete |
| lazydev | source with `group_index = 0` | `per_filetype.lua = { inherit_defaults = true, 'lazydev' }`, provider `module = 'lazydev.integrations.blink', score_offset = 100` | small |

| gitignore, sshconfig, gitcommit, dictionary | own cmp sources (`source:complete(params, callback)`) | same logic as blink sources: `get_completions(ctx, callback)`, kinds from `blink.cmp.types`, `per_filetype` instead of `cmp.setup.filetype` | medium: four ports, mostly renames |

| cmdline | cmp-cmdline: `<Tab>`/`<S-Tab>` open and select, `<C-j>`/`<C-k>` while open, `<Down>`/`<Up>` always history; `/` `?` buffer words | built in; `cmdline.keymap` with `<C-j>` = `{ 'select_next', 'fallback' }`, `<Down>` = `{ 'cancel', 'fallback' }`; per-cmdtype sources through a `sources` function on `vim.fn.getcmdtype()` | medium: the `<Down>` close-then-history needs a check |
| appearance | winblend, winhighlight, lspkind symbols | `completion.menu.winblend`, `.winhighlight`, `.draw.columns`; blink ships its own kind icons (lspkind not needed) | small |

The dictionary source's prefix index stays as it is. blink filters by keyword itself, so `get_completions` should return all words of the two-letter bucket (or the prefix matches, to keep the list small) with `is_incomplete_forward = true`.
## Outside the plugin
- `plug-wip/genja-ask.nvim/lua/genja-ask/init.lua`: `cmp.setup.buffer({ enabled = false })` becomes `vim.b[buf].completion = false`. Both can stay during the switch.
- `lua/lazyp/langs/php-laravel.lua`: blade-nav.nvim lists `hrsh7th/nvim-cmp` as a dependency; it has its own blink source (`blade-nav.integrations.blink`), see Decisions.
- `lua/lazyp/langs-comps/copilot.lua`: comments say nvim-cmp owns `<Tab>`; copilot.vim's ghost text is independent.
- genja-commit's CLAUDE.md: "`<CR>` confirms only a selected item" holds only with `preselect = false`.
- `lua/lazyp/new/genja-comp011.lua`: dependency `hrsh7th/nvim-cmp` becomes `saghen/blink.cmp` (`version = '1.*'`). `lua/lazyp/langs-comps/nvim-cmp.lua` and the cmp-* specs get `-- not used: 2026-10`.

- `tests/comps011/test_comps011.lua` (cmp group): `cmp.complete()` / `cmp.get_entries()` / `e.source.name == 'nvim_lsp'` become `require('blink.cmp').show()` and the list module's items with `source_id == 'lsp'`. The exact accessor needs checking in blink's source before rewriting.
## Suggested order
1. Spec: add blink next to nvim-cmp, `enabled = false` on one side, switched by an option in `local.lua`, so going back is one line.
2. Port init, keymaps, appearance and the built-ins; delete snippets, lsp, path, buffer.
3. Port the four own sources; one commit each.
4. cmdline last: it differs the most from the cmp-cmdline setup.
5. Tests: the cmp group against blink; `make D=comps011 G=cmp`.
6. Remove nvim-cmp and the cmp-* plugins once a week of daily use shows no gaps.
Rough size: about 300 lines changed in `lua/genja/completion/`, plus the test helper. Nothing in the LSP half beyond the capabilities block.
- `<CR>`: blink's default (first item preselected, `<CR>` accepts it). Keymaps file keeps the old behaviour as a commented-out block:
```lua
-- old nvim-cmp behaviour: nothing preselected, <CR> accepts only an item picked with <Tab>
-- opts.completion = { list = { selection = { preselect = false, auto_insert = true } } }
-- opts.keymap['<CR>'] = { 'accept', 'fallback' }
genja-commit's CLAUDE.md bullet ("`<CR>` confirms only a selected item") changes with it.
- Fuzzy matcher: the fastest, the prebuilt Rust one: `version = '1.*'`, `fuzzy = { implementation = 'prefer_rust_with_warning' }` (warns and falls back to Lua if the dll is missing).
- blade-nav (Laravel only: `gf` on Blade directives, components, routes, views; completes `<x-` components and `route('` names): has its own blink source, no blink.compat:

`providers['blade-nav'] = { name = 'blade-nav', module = 'blade-nav.integrations.blink' }`, listed in `per_filetype` for `blade` and `php`. Its spec drops the `hrsh7th/nvim-cmp` dependency (upstream marks it optional).

# cut genja-completion011 startup cost
Status: In Progress (backlog TASK-213)
## Why
On 2026-11-27 the config got startup profiling (`Makefile.startup.mk`: `make startup`,
`startup-cold`, `startup-jitprof-plugins N=5`, per-plugin trees). After the treesitter and Defender
fixes, genja-completion011 is the largest single item in a start:
- warm: ~74 ms of its own code, ~138 ms with what it loads (lazy profile)
- cold, Defender exclusions in place: ~114 ms own, ~361 ms total; ~480 ms in a later cold run
- before the `nvim-data` exclusion: 1.58 s cold, since every module it pulls in was scanned
It loads at VeryLazy and on `BufReadPre`/`BufNewFile`, so it runs after the first screen but before
nvim takes input. On an empty start it sets up all of LSP and Mason just so the command line has
completion. Two fixes are already in (2026-11-27): nvim-lint no longer loads it at setup for a WSL
distro lookup, and the installed servers are enabled in one `vim.lsp.enable(list)` call instead of
one per server (each call re-ran FileType on every buffer, ~15 ms).
The goal: an empty start pays only for completion, a start with a file pays for the LSP of that
file's filetype, and neither notices Mason unless something is missing.
## What the profiles showed
Measured, single runs unless noted:
- mason-lspconfig's `get_installed_package_names()` and its name map: ~17 ms warm. They run at
setup because `ensure_installed` and the enable step need the installed list
- the mason modules themselves (`mason-core.functional`, `mason-registry`, installers): ~165 ms cold
in total, before the Defender fix; still the largest group cold
- `require mason-lspconfig.lsp.autotools_ls`: 21 ms cold for one module, the `make` language
- blink.cmp: 40-60 ms cold; `blink.cmp.fuzzy.download.files` alone ~22 ms cold, the prebuilt matcher
check
- `[string]:spawn` was 6% of one start's samples in plain jit.p; something starts a process during
startup. Not yet traced to its caller
Suspected, not measured:
- `load_lang()` and `load_config()` call `nvim_get_runtime_file()` for every enabled language and
for `local.lua`: a runtimepath scan each, about 20 per start. `pcall(require, ...)` searches the
same path and could replace the check
- `install_tools()` and mason-lspconfig's `setup()` both call `registry.refresh()` at start; on a
machine with everything installed that is work for nothing, and possibly the `spawn`
- the ~114 ms (cold) of genja-completion011's own code is not yet split by line; the `self` column
of `make startup-jitprof-plugins` now does that
## The idea
Split the plugin's start into what the first keypress needs and what the first file needs.
1. Completion first, LSP later. blink.cmp and the command line sources load at VeryLazy (or
`CmdlineEnter`, `InsertEnter`); servers, Mason and mason-lspconfig load on the first `FileType`
that has an enabled server. An empty start then sets up no LSP at all.
2. Mason only when needed. Read the installed servers once from `mason/packages/` (a directory
listing) and enable them; call `registry.refresh()`, `ensure_installed` and `install_tools()`
only when a wanted package is missing, and then after a delay (`vim.defer_fn`), so installs never
compete with the first screen. `:Mason`, `:MasonInstall` and `:checkhealth` still load the full
thing.
3. Per-language work on demand. Language modules are loaded when collecting servers; anything heavier
in them (WSL lookups, project detection) moves into `root_dir`, `before_init` or the server's
first attach. The mason-lspconfig overrides (`mason-lspconfig.lsp.<name>`) are required only for
the servers being enabled, on their filetype.
4. Fewer runtimepath scans. Replace `nvim_get_runtime_file()` checks before `require` with the
`require` itself, keeping the warning for a missing language file.
5. Find the `spawn`. Trace it with `make startup-jitprof-full` (it shows nvim's own frames) and move
it out of startup or drop it.
Each step is measured before and after with `make startup-jitprof-plugins N=5` (median, self
column) and `make startup-cold`, and noted in the task.
## Impact
- genja-completion011: `comps/init.lua` (order and triggers), `lsp/init.lua` (installed list,
refresh and installs deferred, overrides per server), `lang/*.lua` where a module does work at
load, CLAUDE.md
- config: `lua/lazyp/new/genja-completion011.lua` triggers (VeryLazy for completion, FileType for
LSP), maybe split into two specs
- tests: the config's `tests/comps011` groups `lsp`, `ready`, `mason` and `cmp` must pass as before;
`ready` covers the first-file attach, which the split moves
- risk: a server must still attach to the first file opened from the command line
(`nvim foo.php`); FileType for that buffer can fire before the LSP part is set up, so setup has to
enable for the buffers already open (as `vim.lsp.enable()` does after `vim_did_enter`)
# a history mode with stacked branches
Status: To Do (backlog TASK-190). Open proposal, decided in part (see Decided). Project: frontend (Ops).
## Why
Agents now build work as **stacked branches**: one branch per task, each started from the one
before it, several stacks in parallel worktrees, joined and merged in a fixed order later. In
Purrage on 2026-11-17 that was 21 branches in four stacks (A, B, C built in parallel, D after the
join), with the order kept by hand in an ASCII tree, in the task files and in commit trailers.
Ops can show one pair of branches as a pull request, but nothing shows the *shape*: which branch
sits on which, which one is next to merge, which stack still needs a rebase, which agent is still
building, and what each one reported. The user had to ask for the tree again and again while the
agents worked, and the merge order lived in a hand-written note
(`Purrage/doc-wip/readme.2026-11-17.merge-order.md`, where this idea started).
## What Changes
A new **History** mode on the rail (4th, after Pull request, Changes and Add and Ignore; the rail is Alt+1 … Alt+9, see
`purrage-mode-and-ui`). This proposal
specifies its first view, **Stack**; a commit log view can follow in the same mode.
### Where the stack comes from
Everything is read from the active directory's repository; nothing new has to be recorded.
- **Ancestry** draws the tree: each local branch hangs under the nearest other local branch that
is its ancestor (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`), and the root is the default branch.
- **Intent** comes from the `Stacked-On:` commit trailer (and `Task:`), read from the branch's
commits. When ancestry and intent disagree (a parent was rewritten, a stack is not rebased
yet) the row is marked and shows both, e.g. "trailer: PR-keys-every-mode · ancestry: main".
- **Order**: the merge position from the task file's `Merge N of M` line, when there is one;
otherwise the order of ancestry.
- **Worktrees**: `git worktree list --porcelain`: where a branch is checked out, locked or not;
`git status` there: dirty or clean.
- **Agent information**: the task linked by the `Task:` trailer, read through the Tasks mode's
Backlog reader: status, ACs ticked (`5/7`), and the `## Notes` section.
All **local** branches are shown; a `PR-*` prefix is not special.
### What a row shows
History ▸ Stack                                            watching refs ●
main @ v2-solidify
├─ ✔ 1  PR-background-work-handle   task-19  Done 3/3          merged
├─ ▶ 2  PR-process-env-seams        task-15  Done 3/3   +4 −0  next  [merge]
│  └─ ○ 3  PR-workspace-out-of-shell task-14 Done 3/3   +9      waiting
│     └─ ⚠ 7 PR-time-the-actions     task-1   Done 4/4          trailer: PR-keys-every-mode,
│                                                                ancestry: main  [restack]
└─ ⟳ 13 PR-design-tokens             task-20  In Progress 5/7   dirty · stack-b
Enter: review against parent   m: base ↔ main   M: merge next   R: restack
- merge position, branch, task id and title, task status and ACs;
- state, each with an icon and a word, never colour alone: **merged** into the default branch ·
**next** (merging it is a fast-forward) · **waiting** · **needs restack** (its parent moved, or
ancestry and trailer disagree) · **being built** (its worktree is dirty, or it has no commit
of its own yet);
- commits and files ahead of its parent;
- worktree: folder name, locked, dirty;
- the task's Notes expand under the row (a disclosure, closed by default).
### What it does
- **Review**: `Enter` opens the Pull request mode with *base = the row's parent, head = the
branch*, so the diff is only that task's change. `m` toggles the base between the parent and
the default branch, there and back.
- **Merge next** (`M`): fast-forwards the default branch to the next branch in order. Offered only
when it is a fast-forward, so it cannot conflict. Local only; nothing is pushed.
- **Restack** (`R`): rebases the children of a parent that moved onto it, one branch at a time in
stack order, with `--update-refs`. It stops at the first conflict and hands it to the conflict
layout the Pull request merge already uses; a stopped restack can be continued or aborted there.
Before it starts, Ops tags the old tips (`pre-restack-<branch>`), so nothing can be lost.
- Every action answers with a short note, as the Pull request actions do.
### How live
The view **watches refs**: a file watcher on `.git/HEAD`, `.git/refs/`, `.git/packed-refs` and each
worktree's `HEAD` and `index`. When an agent commits, switches branch or rebases, the view
re-reads (debounced) and redraws only the rows that changed. No timer, no polling. The watcher is
the local backend's repository watcher (TASK-186), not a second one.
## Decided (2026-11-17, the user)
| question | answer |
| Where | a view in a new **History** mode, not a mode of its own and not inside Pull request |
| Source of the order | **both** ancestry and the `Stacked-On:` trailer; disagreement is shown |
| Which branches | **all local** branches |
| Review base | **toggle**: parent by default, `m` switches to the default branch |
| Actions | **merge next** (fast-forward only) and **restack** (stop at the first conflict) |
| Liveness | **watch refs** (file watcher), no timer |
| Agent information | **yes**, from the task file: status, ACs, Notes |
## Open questions
- The History mode's other view: a commit log (graph or flat), and which is shown first.
- Branches without a task or trailer (plain feature branches): one flat group, or by ancestry
like the rest.
- Merging a whole stack at once (fast-forward to its tip) as well as "next".
- Whether restack also updates the `Stacked-On:` trailer of a commit whose parent changed
(that rewrites the message; today the trailer keeps saying where it was built).
- Keys: `m` / `M` / `R` against the existing table (`M-…` is Alt); check for clashes.
## Impact
- New: `lib/ui/history_view.dart` (mode), `lib/ui/stack_view.dart`; `lib/state/stack.dart`
(the model: branches, ancestry, trailers, worktrees, task link) with unit tests on fixture git
output; ref changes from the repository watcher (TASK-186).
- Changed: mode rail and Alt+1 … Alt+9, Help key table, the Pull request mode (open with a given
base and head, base toggle), the Tasks reader (look a task up by id).
- Git commands used: `for-each-ref`, `merge-base --is-ancestor`, `log --format=%(trailers…)`,
`worktree list --porcelain`, `status --porcelain`, `merge --ff-only`, `rebase --update-refs`,
`tag`. Nothing pushes.
- PLAN.md: a "History" section under Views (Modes), and the rail order.

# a board mode for the changes
Status: Open proposal, not decided. There is no backlog task yet; one gets made if we go ahead.
## Why
The Tasks mode lists the OpenSpec changes and the Backlog.md tasks, grouped and sorted. A list
answers "what is there", but not "where is each change". To see that, I open a change and read its
checkboxes. With a handful of changes that is fine; with twenty, some drafted last week by an agent,
some half built, some waiting for a tasks file, I want one picture: which changes are only an idea,
which are ready to build, which are being built, which are done and waiting to be archived.
A Kanban board is that picture. The npm package `specdeck` shows one for OpenSpec projects, and it
is a good one. I do not want to run it or depend on it: it is a Node server with a browser page,
and this app already has everything such a board needs, in Dart, inside the window I work in. What I
want is the same kind of board as a mode of Ops, built by reading how `specdeck` decides things and
doing the same in our own code.
## What I learned from the specdeck source
I read the source of `specdeck` 0.4.1 (MIT) without running it. These are the parts that matter
here.
**Lanes are never stored.** A change has no status field. Its lane is worked out from the files
every time: which artifacts exist and how many task boxes are ticked. The board can therefore never
disagree with the repository, and an agent that ticks a box in `tasks.md` moves the card without
anyone telling the board. The lanes, in order: Draft, Proposed, Specified, Ready, In Progress, Done,
Archived.
**The rule that places a card** is short:
- in the archive folder: Archived;
- `tasks.md` exists: no boxes, or none ticked: Ready; all ticked: Done; some ticked: In Progress;
- no `tasks.md`, and no artifact at all: Draft;
- no `tasks.md`, and everything `tasks.md` depends on is written (proposal, design, specs): Specified;
- otherwise: Proposed.
It does not name `proposal.md` or `tasks.md` in the rule. It asks the workflow schema which artifact
tracks the implementation and what that artifact needs, so a project with its own schema still gets
sensible lanes.
**An artifact is done when its file exists.** There is no judgement of quality. A one-line proposal
counts. An artifact whose dependencies are missing is blocked, otherwise it is ready to write.
**Tasks are only checkboxes.** `- [ ] 1.1 text`, under `## 1. Heading`. Plain bullets are not
tracked, and a tasks file full of bullets with no boxes is reported as a problem instead of showing
an empty list. A checkbox before any heading still counts.
**A board never moves a card by hand.** Dragging a card between lanes is refused by design, because
the next read of the files would undo it. The one drag that exists is archiving, because that is a
real action.
**Writes are narrow.** The only thing it writes is a task checkbox, and the write is refused when the
file changed since it was read.
Everything else in `specdeck` (the server, the browser editor, approval by git trailers, handing work
to an agent, a registry of projects) is a product around that board, and is not part of this
proposal.
## Backlog.md's board, to analyze later
Backlog.md, whose task files the Tasks mode already reads, has a Kanban board of its own. It is not
analyzed here, and nothing in this proposal is based on it. Before anything is built, its source
gets the same treatment as `specdeck`'s: read, not run, and written down in this proposal the way
the section above does. The questions to take to it:
- how a task lands in a column: from its `status` field, so the board shows a stored state, unlike
`specdeck`'s derived one;
- which columns there are, whether they come from `backlog/config.yml`, and how they are ordered;
- how cards are ordered inside a column (the `ordinal` field), and what moving a card writes;
- what a card shows, and how milestones, labels and filters work on the board;
- what it does with many tasks and with tasks from several projects.
The two boards answer different questions. Backlog.md's says where a task is, by what someone
recorded. `specdeck`'s says where a change is, by what its files show. This app has both kinds of
thing, tasks and changes, so the Board mode may need a switch between the two, or one board with the
change's lane and the task's status side by side. That is decided after both are understood.
## The idea
A new mode, the Board, between Tasks and Directories on the rail. It shows the changes of the Active
Directory's planning folder as columns, one per lane, left to right in the order above. Each change
is a card: its name, how many boxes are ticked out of how many, and the Backlog.md task it belongs to
when it has one. A lane with nothing in it stays visible but thin.
The lanes are derived in Dart from the files the Tasks mode already loads (`Workspace`): the
proposal, design, spec deltas and tasks of each change, and whether it sits in the archive. Nothing
new is stored and nothing new is read from disk. When a file changes, in Neovim or outside it, the
workspace reloads and the card moves, the way every other mode follows the backend.
The board does not invent a status. It also does not replace the status of the Backlog.md task: a
task's To Do, In Progress and Done stay where they are, in the Tasks mode. A card can show its
task's status as a small mark, but the lane comes from the change's files alone. Where the two
disagree, for instance a task marked Done whose change is still In Progress, the card says so; that
disagreement is useful to see.
Clicking a card opens the same change detail as in the Tasks mode, in a panel from the right.
Ticking a box there already works and already refuses a stale file, so a card moves in front of me
when I tick the last box.
## Use cases
Each case is written from where I sit.
### Where is everything
I switch to the Board. Seven columns. Draft has two cards an agent started last night: a proposal
and nothing else. Specified has one: proposal, design and specs are written, but no task list yet.
Ready has three, In Progress two, Done one, and Archived is folded to a thin strip because I rarely
want it. I see that three changes are ready to build and nobody has started them, which is the thing
I came to find out.
### A card moves by itself
An agent works through `tasks.md` of a change that is In Progress. I leave the Board open. As the
last box is ticked, the card moves from In Progress to Done. Nobody pressed anything on the board.
### Why is this card here
A change sits in Proposed although I think I wrote everything. I open it and see that the design
is missing; the card shows that the lane is Proposed because `design.md` does not exist yet, not
because someone decided so. I write the file in Neovim and the card moves to Specified.
### A tasks file with no boxes
An agent wrote `tasks.md` with plain bullets. The card sits in Ready and shows a warning: the file
has bullets but no checkboxes, so none of it counts as progress. This is better than a card that
claims nothing has been started.
### Dragging
I try to drag a card from Ready to Done. Nothing moves, and a short note says lanes come from the
files. Dragging a Done card to Archived is the exception and asks first, like archiving in the Tasks
mode does today.
## How it could fit the app
This section is the technical side, and is a first guess.
- `lib/tasks/lanes.dart`: a pure function from a change's artifacts and task counts to a lane,
with the rule above, and unit tests. The artifacts and the task counts are in the model already
(`parse.dart`, `model.dart`).
- `lib/ui/board_view.dart`: the mode. The columns are a horizontal list of lists built from data,
with named sub-widgets for the lane and the card, following `declarative_ui_guidelines.md`.
- The rail gets a sixth mode, so `M-1` to `M-5` become `M-1` to `M-6`; the Keys table, the Help
mode and the debug bar's role table get the new entries.
- Keys, in the pane and list vocabulary of the other modes: Left and Right (`h`, `l`) between lanes,
Up and Down (`j`, `k`) between cards, past the last lane Right goes nowhere, Left from the first
lane goes to the rail, Enter opens the detail, Esc closes it, `gg` and `G` first and last card.
The Tab cycle: the rail, then the lanes, then the detail.
- The workflow schema: OpenSpec projects can have their own. A first version assumes the default
(`tasks.md` tracks the work, and needs the proposal, design and specs). Reading the schema file
to find the tracked artifact is a second step.
- Performance: the lanes are derived when the workspace loads or reloads, not in `build`. Moving a
card is a re-derivation of that one change.
Taking ideas from `specdeck` is fine under its MIT licence. We write our own code, and the
proposal's text names it as the source of the lane rule and the "nothing is stored" principle.
## Open questions
- Should the Archived lane exist at all, or is archiving a change in the Tasks mode enough?
- Should a card show its Backlog.md task's status, or only the change's own progress?
- The lane names: `specdeck` uses Draft, Proposed, Specified, Ready, In Progress, Done, Archived.
Ours could be closer to the Tasks mode's words (To Do, In Progress, Needs Test, Done). The
derivation does not depend on the names.
- One board for the whole planning folder, or a project filter like the Tasks mode has (`a` toggles
every project's changes).
- Whether to look at git as well: a change that exists on another branch only, or has uncommitted
edits, is something `specdeck` marks on the card. The Pull request and Changes modes already know
git, so this could come later.
# Tasks
Only if the proposal is accepted.

- [ ] 1.1 decide the open questions in the proposal (lane names, Archived lane, task status on the card)

# treesitter parsers per enabled language
Status: In Progress (backlog TASK-212)
## Why
Languages are switched on in one place: the `enabled` table of genja-completion011, merged with the
machine's `lua/genja/lsp/local.lua`. Treesitter parsers are listed in another: a fixed list of about
forty names in the config's `lua/lazyp/my/load-treesitter.lua`. The two drift apart. Today the list
installs `vue`, `svelte`, `astro`, `angular`, `templ` and `blade` on a machine where none of those
languages is on, and it has no `c`, `cpp` or `python`, although `c_cpp` and `python` are language
modules and python is on here. The language modules already say this in comments ("treesitter vue
is in the config's load-treesitter.lua"), which is the sign that the list belongs with them.
Switching a language on should bring everything it needs, the parsers included, the same way it
already brings its servers and Mason tools. Switching one off should stop installing its parsers,
so a new machine only builds what it uses; every parser is a C build at first install.
## The idea
Each language module names its parsers next to its servers and tools:
```lua
-- lua/genja/lang/go.lua
return {
servers = { gopls = { ... } },
tools = { 'golangci-lint' },
parsers = { 'go', 'gomod', 'gosum', 'gotmpl', 'templ', 'proto' },
Completion features that work on a filetype name theirs too (`gitcommit`: `gitcommit`, `git_rebase`,
`diff`; `gitignore`: `gitignore`, `gitattributes`; `sshconfig`: `ssh_config`). A short base list is
always installed, because Neovim itself and the config use it whatever is enabled: `lua`, `vim`,
`vimdoc`, `markdown`, `markdown_inline`, `regex`, `query`. Neovim ships most of these (and `c`), but
nvim-treesitter's queries expect its own builds of them, so they stay in the list.
genja-completion011 collects the parsers of the enabled languages and features the way it collects
servers and tools, and exposes the list as `require('genja.lsp').parsers()`. Treesitter itself stays
in the config's spec, which keeps loading at start so highlighting works on the first buffer; only
its scheduled `install_parsers()` changes. It installs `parsers()` plus a short list of the config's
own (`yaml` for `yaml.ansible`, `xml`), instead of the fixed list. The compiler check and the PATH

# merge beside the checkout
Status: In Progress (backlog TASK-143). The open questions were answered on 2026-11-14 (see Decisions).
Rescanned 2026-11-19: built in the relay (merge without a checkout, the checkout brought forward,
the refusal on unsaved buffers, the merge worktree) and in Ops (the merge button, its notes, the
rules in PLAN.md); its backlog tasks still say To Do and need checking against the code and a test.
The work is in backlog tasks, not in a tasks.md: TASK-143 clean merge without a checkout, TASK-144
bring the checkout forward, TASK-145 refuse on unsaved buffers, TASK-146 merge worktree for
conflicts, TASK-147 dialogs and notes in Ops, TASK-148 merge rules in PLAN.md.
## Why
The PR mode has a Merge button. It merges the head branch into the base branch with a merge commit,
and nothing is pushed. To do that today, it uses the main checkout: the folder where I normally
work and where Neovim has my files open. If base is not the branch checked out there, Merge
checks it out first. Merge also refuses to start while there are unsaved buffers or uncommitted
changes to tracked files. A merge in a dirty folder can mix my unfinished edits into the merge, or
fail halfway and leave both tangled together.
That rule is safe, but it gets in the way of the most common case. Most days, the main checkout is
on `main` and has something in progress: a half-written README section, a config value I am trying
out, or files an agent is editing. Meanwhile a finished branch is waiting, say
`feature/api-integration`, which an agent built in its own worktree. All I want is to put that
branch into `main`. Today I first have to commit or stash my unrelated work, merge, and then get my
work back. The merge has nothing to do with the files I am editing, but the folder is dirty, so I
am stopped.
The other case is just as awkward. Say I am working on `feature/cms-updates` in the main checkout,
and I want to merge `feature/api-integration` into `main`. Merge would switch the main checkout to
`main`, right where Neovim has my `feature/cms-updates` files open. Even if that works, it is not
what I asked for. I wanted `main` to move forward, not to be taken off my own branch.
So the goal is this: merging a finished branch into `main` should not need the main checkout to be
clean, and it should not switch branches or leave conflict markers there. The main checkout belongs
to me while I work. The merge should happen somewhere else.
## The idea
Most merges are clean: the two branches changed different files, or different parts of the same
file. Git can work out such a merge entirely by itself, without writing a single file on disk. It
does the merge in its own storage, makes the merge commit there, and then moves `main` to point at
it. No folder has to be checked out and no files are written, so nobody's work is in the way. When
Ops moves `main`, it first checks that `main` is still where it was when the merge started. If
someone else committed to `main` in the meantime, the merge is not saved, nothing is lost, and Ops
offers to rebase `fix/login-timeout` onto the new `main` and then merge it; I confirm it. Rebase is
the preferred outcome, so `main` keeps one straight line of history.
Some merges have conflicts: both branches changed the same lines. Those can't be finished without a
place to resolve them, where someone opens the files with conflict markers, fixes them and commits.
That place should not be my main checkout. So Ops makes a merge worktree of its own, one per PR
branch, in the temp folder: `%TEMP%\nvimos-ops\merge.<repo>.<branch>`, for example
`merge.nvimos-poc-frontend.feature-api-integration`. The names start with `merge` so they are easy
to spot as a group. The conflicted merge waits there for me. `main` does not move until the
conflict is resolved and committed, and my main checkout never sees a conflict marker. Once the
merge is committed or thrown away, Ops removes the worktree.
One step is left when `main` is the branch checked out in my main checkout. Moving the branch does
not change the files on disk. Right after the merge, my folder still shows the old `main`, and git
would think I had undone everything the merge brought in. So Ops brings the folder forward to the
new `main`, the same way git does when switching between two commits: it rewrites the files the
merge changed and leaves every other file alone, including my uncommitted edits. After that, Neovim
reloads any open buffer whose file changed, so I see the merged text.
The tricky part is a file that the merge changed and that I am also editing. Then the merged
version and my unfinished version would have to be mixed in my folder, which is exactly what we
want to avoid. Ops asks me first, in a dialog that lists those files; the use cases below describe
it. A buffer with unsaved changes on such a file is different: Merge refuses before anything
happens.
This is the fallback, not a replacement. When the main checkout is already on the base branch and
clean, Merge works as it does today. The new path takes over only where today's Merge would
refuse or switch my branch.
In short: a clean merge happens without a folder, a merge with conflicts happens in Ops's own
merge folder, and the main checkout is never switched to another branch. At most, it is brought
forward to the new `main` when that is the branch it is on.
## Use cases
Each case is written from where I sit: what I do, what I see, and which part of the idea handles
it. The branches are an ordinary week's work: `main`; two finished branches, `feature/api-integration`
and `fix/login-timeout`; and `feature/cms-updates`, which I am still writing.
### Merging into main while I have unrelated work in progress
The main checkout is on `main`. I have uncommitted edits in `README.md` and `config/dev.yaml`. An
agent has finished `feature/api-integration`, which adds files under `lib/api/` and changes
`lib/client.dart`. In the PR mode I pick base `main` and head `feature/api-integration`, look at the
diff, press Merge and confirm.
Today, Merge refuses because the folder is dirty. With this proposal, the merge is clean, so git
does it without a folder, `main` moves, and my main checkout is brought forward. I see the short
note "Merged feature/api-integration into main", and the lists refresh. `lib/api/` and the new
`lib/client.dart` are on disk, and if I had `lib/client.dart` open in Neovim, the buffer now shows
the merged text. My README and config edits are still there, uncommitted and untouched.
### Merging into main while I work on another branch
The main checkout is on `feature/cms-updates`, my own branch, with open buffers and some unsaved
work. `fix/login-timeout` is done, and I want it in `main`. I pick base `main` and head
`fix/login-timeout`, and press Merge.
Today, Merge would switch my folder to `main` and take me off my branch. With this proposal, `main`
is not checked out anywhere, so no files need to change at all. The merge happens without a
folder, and `main` moves. My checkout, my branch and my buffers are left completely alone. I see the
same short note, and `main` in the pickers now contains the fix.
### The merge changes a file I am editing
As in the first case, but this time my uncommitted edits are in `lib/client.dart`, the same file
`feature/api-integration` changes. The merge itself is clean, but bringing my folder forward would
have to mix the merged `lib/client.dart` with my unfinished edits.
Before anything happens, Ops shows a dialog. It lists the affected files, here `lib/client.dart`,
and offers four ways on:
- **Stash, apply, pop** (the default): my edits to those files go into a stash, the folder is
brought forward, and the stash is applied on top. If it applies cleanly, the stash is dropped.
If my edits and the merge touched the same lines, the file gets conflict markers and the stash
is kept, so nothing is lost.
- **Discard modified files**: my edits to those files are thrown away and the folder is brought
forward.
- **Move main only**: `main` moves, my folder stays behind with a note, and I bring it forward
when my edit is done.
- **Refuse**: nothing happens.
My other uncommitted edits, in `README.md` and `config/dev.yaml`, are left alone in every case.
### The merge changes a file with unsaved changes in Neovim
As above, but I have `lib/client.dart` open in Neovim with unsaved changes. Ops never overwrites
such a buffer, so Merge refuses up front. The note names the path and the buffer number, for
example "lib/client.dart (buffer 7) has unsaved changes, and the merge changes it", and has a
button that opens that buffer in a new tab, so I can save or drop the changes and merge again.
### The merge has conflicts
`feature/cms-updates` and `feature/api-integration` both changed `config/routes.yaml`. The API
branch was merged yesterday. Today I merge `feature/cms-updates` into `main`, and the two changes to
the routes file overlap.
Today, Merge undoes the merge, lists the files, and that is the end of it. With this proposal, Ops
finds out about the conflict without having touched anything, then runs the merge in its own merge
folder and leaves it there. I see a note that the merge stopped on a conflict in
`config/routes.yaml`, with a way to open it or throw it away. My main checkout and `main` itself
are exactly as before. Once I have fixed the file in the merge folder and committed, `main` moves to
the merge commit. If my main checkout is on `main`, it is brought forward as in the first case.
### Main moved while I was deciding
I opened the merge question for `fix/login-timeout`, and while it was open, an agent committed a
small fix straight to `main`. I press Yes.
The merge was worked out against the old `main`, so Ops does not save it. Nothing is lost: the
agent's commit stays on `main`, and no merge commit is stored. I see a note that `main` changed
during the merge and offers the rebase; if I confirm, the branch is rebased onto the new `main`, then
merged, and the diff refreshes to it.
### Nothing in progress
The main checkout is clean and on `main`. Merge works exactly as it does today; the new path is
not used. That keeps the risk low while the new path is young.
## How it works in git
This section is the technical side of the idea above. The git here is 2.46. `merge-tree
--write-tree` needs 2.38 or later.
### A clean merge, without a work tree
`git merge-tree --write-tree` merges two commits in the object database. It writes no files and
uses no index. On success it prints the id of the merged tree and exits 0. On a conflict it exits 1,
and the output lists the conflicted files.
```sh
old=$(git rev-parse refs/heads/main)
head=$(git rev-parse refs/heads/feature/api-integration)
tree=$(git merge-tree --write-tree "$old" "$head")      # exit 1: conflict, see below
commit=$(git commit-tree "$tree" -p "$old" -p "$head" \
-m "Merge branch 'feature/api-integration'")
git update-ref -m "ops: merge feature/api-integration" refs/heads/main "$commit" "$old"
The last argument of `update-ref` is the value `main` must still have. If someone moved `main`
in the meantime, `update-ref` fails, and the new commit is simply an unreferenced object that `gc`
cleans up later. That is the "Main moved while I was deciding" case.
The merge commit gets the usual author and committer from `user.name` and `user.email`. Hooks do
not run (`commit-tree` is plumbing), which matches today's Merge closely enough, since it runs no
hooks of its own either. That is worth checking.
### Bringing the main checkout forward
When `main` is checked out in the main checkout (`git symbolic-ref HEAD` is `refs/heads/main`
there), the files on disk still match `$old` after `update-ref`. A two-tree read moves the index
and the work tree from `$old` to `$commit`, changing only the paths that differ between the two,
which is what `git checkout` does:
```sh
git read-tree -m -u "$old" "$commit"
It refuses, and changes nothing, if a path that differs between the two trees also has changes in
the index or the work tree. That is the "file I am editing" case. To ask before anything moves,
check first:
```sh
git diff --name-only "$old" "$commit"         # files the merge changes
git status --porcelain=v1 -z                  # files I have touched
# overlap -> the dialog, listing the files
The dialog's choices, with `$files` the overlapping paths:
```sh
# stash, apply, pop (default)
git stash push -m "ops: merge feature/api-integration" -- $files
git update-ref refs/heads/main "$commit" "$old"
git read-tree -m -u "$old" "$commit"
git stash apply --index && git stash drop     # conflict: markers in $files, stash kept
# discard modified files
git checkout "$old" -- $files                 # back to the committed text, then as usual
# move main only: update-ref, no read-tree; the note says the folder is behind
# refuse: nothing
The stash list is shared by all worktrees; the message `ops: merge <branch>` makes Ops's entry
easy to recognise.
`main` being checked out in some other worktree (an agent's) is found with
`git worktree list --porcelain`. That worktree is left alone: bringing it forward is its owner's
business.
The unsaved-buffer check and the reload happen in Neovim: refuse if a modified buffer's file is in
the `git diff --name-only` list, naming the path and the buffer number, and run `:checktime` after
`read-tree`. Opening the buffer in a new tab is `:tab sbuffer <nr>`.
### A merge with conflicts, in the merge worktree
`main` may not be checked out twice, so the merge worktree uses a detached HEAD:
```sh
repo=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
wt="$TEMP/nvimos-ops/merge.$repo.feature-api-integration"   # '/' and other unsafe chars -> '-'
git worktree add --detach "$wt" "$old"
git -C "$wt" merge --no-ff --no-commit feature/api-integration
# conflicted files: git -C "$wt" diff --name-only --diff-filter=U
After I resolve and stage the files there:
```sh
git -C "$wt" commit --no-edit
git update-ref refs/heads/main "$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse HEAD)" "$old"
git worktree remove "$wt"
# then bring the main checkout forward, as above
Throwing the conflict away is `git -C "$wt" merge --abort` and `git worktree remove "$wt"`. The
temp folder can be cleaned out by Windows or a cleanup tool; then `git worktree prune` forgets the
worktree and Ops makes it again. A half-resolved conflict is lost with it, which is a known risk.
### Later actions
A fast-forward is `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$old" "$head"` followed by `update-ref` to `$head`
and the same bringing forward. A squash is `merge-tree` and `commit-tree` with one parent (`-p
"$old"` only). A rebase really needs a work tree and would be the merge worktree's second job.
## Decisions
Answered on 2026-11-14:
- **The merge worktree stays.** A conflict is one click in Ops, not a trip to the terminal.
- **It lives in the temp folder**, one per PR branch: `%TEMP%\nvimos-ops\merge.<repo>.<branch>`,
removed once the merge is committed or thrown away.
- **A merge that changes a file I am editing** opens a dialog listing the files: stash, apply, pop
(default), discard modified files, move main only, or refuse.
- **An unsaved buffer on a merged file** makes Merge refuse up front, naming the path and the
buffer number, with a button that opens the buffer in a new tab.
- **`main` checked out in an agent's worktree** is left alone.
- **The new path is the fallback**, used only where today's Merge would refuse or switch my
branch. A clean main checkout on base merges as today.
- **The backend runs the git commands** (`git.merge` in relay), next to the buffer check and the
reload.
Still to check: the merge commit made with `commit-tree` runs no hooks.
## Impact
In the backend, `git.merge` (relay, branch `PR-merge-action`) gains the folder-less merge, the
guarded branch move, bringing the main checkout forward with the stash and discard choices, the
unsaved-buffer refusal with buffer numbers, and the merge worktree. In the frontend,
`PrState.canMerge` and `PrState.merge` in `lib/state/pr.dart` stop refusing a dirty folder as a
whole, `lib/ui/pr_view.dart` gains the affected-files dialog, the "open buffer in a new tab"
button, and the conflict and "main moved" notes. The merge rules in `PLAN.md` are rewritten to match.
## ADDED Requirements
Draft, for discussion; nothing here is decided.
### Requirement: Merge leaves the main checkout alone
A merge of head into base SHALL NOT switch branches or write conflict markers in the main checkout.
#### Scenario: Base is checked out and dirty
- **WHEN** base is checked out in the main checkout, which has uncommitted changes in files the merge
does not touch, and the user merges head into base
- **THEN** base gets the merge commit, the main checkout is on the new commit, and the uncommitted
changes are still there
#### Scenario: Base moved meanwhile
- **WHEN** base gets a new commit while the merge runs
- **THEN** the merge fails and base keeps the new commit
### Requirement: Conflicts are resolved beside the checkout
A merge with conflicts SHALL stop in the merge worktree, not in the main checkout.
#### Scenario: Conflict
- **WHEN** head and base change the same lines
- **THEN** Ops names the conflicted files, the main checkout has no conflict markers, and base has

# merge conflict view
Status: In Progress (backlog TASK-151 to TASK-153). Builds on `merge-beside-checkout` (TASK-143 to TASK-146)
and TASK-150. Drafted 2026-11-15. Rescanned 2026-11-19: the merge-tree pre-flight, the
conflict-marker checks and finishing in the merge worktree are in the relay's `merge.lua`, the
conflict view is `conflict_view.dart` in Ops; the backlog tasks still say To Do and need checking
against the code and a test.
## Why
Clicking Merge in the pull request view today either merges cleanly or, when the two branches changed
the same lines, undoes the merge and shows an error that names the files. The error tells me what
went wrong but nothing about how to fix it. To finish the merge I have to leave Ops, open each
conflicted file in another tool, fix the lines, come back, and commit somewhere else. The part of
the job that needs the most care is the part Ops does least for me.
The goal is that a conflict becomes something Ops shows and helps me resolve, in the same place where
I started the merge, with the same kind of view I already use for diffs.
## The idea
Merge starts with a pre-flight. Before anything changes, Ops asks git whether the two branches would
conflict, and it does this without writing anything to the repo. A conflict costs nothing to find
out. If there is no conflict, the merge runs as it does now, as described in `merge-beside-checkout`.
If there are conflicts, Ops does not run the merge at all. It opens a third diff mode, the conflict
view, beside the unified and side-by-side modes. The view lists the conflicted files and lets me
resolve them.
The conflict view works on the merge worktree from TASK-146, a separate working folder that Ops keeps
for the merge, not on my main checkout. So my main checkout never sees a conflict marker, and `main`
does not move until the merge is committed.
Within a conflicted file, each hunk shows the two sides, ours and theirs, and I pick one of them for
that hunk. The idea follows Meld, an open source diff tool, which lets the user take either side of a
conflict block. A conflicted file can also be opened in nvim, in a new nvim-qt window on that file
and not in diff mode, for anything the two picks do not cover.
Two guards keep a half-resolved file from getting through. Adding a file, with the add button that
also marks a conflict as resolved, is refused while the file still has conflict markers at the start
of a line. And before the commit that completes the merge, a verify step checks that no conflicted
path is left and that no staged file has a marker. Tests and analysis are optional, not a gate.
When everything passes, the commit completes the merge on `main`.
In short: a conflict is found before anything changes, shown in its own diff mode, resolved per hunk
or in nvim, guarded at add and again at commit, and finished by a merge commit on the base branch.
## Use cases
The cast: I am a developer working on Ops. `feature/api-integration` is a finished branch that an
agent built in its own worktree. `main` is the base. The conflicts I meet are in `config/routes.yaml`
and `PLAN.md`, where both branches changed the same lines.
### Merge with a conflict
I click Merge in the pull request view with `main` as base and `feature/api-integration` as head. The
pre-flight finds two conflicted files, and the conflict view opens on the first one. Nothing asks me
first, the same as a plain merge. Today the same click would have ended in an error that undoes the
merge. The part of the idea that handles it is the pre-flight, and the view it opens.
### Pick a side for one hunk
In `config/routes.yaml` there is one hunk where my branch renamed a route and `main` changed its
timeout. I pick theirs for the rename and ours for the timeout, and the file's preview shows the
combined result. The other hunks stay as they are until I pick them too.
### Open a file in nvim
One hunk in `PLAN.md` needs a real edit that neither side has. I open the file in nvim, in a new
nvim-qt window, edit it, save, and come back to Ops. The conflict view reads the file again, so
what I saved is what I see.
### Try to add a file with markers
I click add on `PLAN.md` while a `<<<<<<<` line is still in it. Ops refuses, names the file and the
line, and the file stays unresolved. The check is the reason the add button is safe to use in a hurry.
### Everything resolved
I add both files. The verify step passes, nothing is left unmerged and no marker is staged, and the
commit completes the merge on `main`. The view says so, and the lists refresh.
### Main moved while I was resolving
While I was resolving, a support engineer committed a fix to `main`. When I click Resolve, Ops runs
the pre-flight again. If the conflict is still there, the view opens with the current files. If the
conflict is gone, the merge goes through as a plain merge and the view says that it did.
### Nothing special
I merge `feature/api-integration` into `main` and there is no conflict. The pre-flight passes, the
merge runs as a plain merge, and no view opens. That case keeps working exactly as it does today.
## How it works in git
The pre-flight reads both branches without changing the repo, and the resolution happens in the merge
worktree, never in the main checkout. Each block below is one part of the idea.
### The pre-flight
git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only --messages <base> <head>
This writes objects to git's store but does not change the working tree, the index or any branch. It
lists the conflicted paths by name. It needs git 2.38 or newer, which this machine has; an older git
needs the three-argument form, which prints its output in a different shape and has to be parsed.
Its result decides the dialog, and the same call runs again when Resolve is clicked, so a commit that
landed in the meantime is not missed.
### Resolving in the merge worktree
git -C "$wt" add <file>          # only after the marker check passes
git -C "$wt" commit              # completes the merge on the detached base
The merge worktree is the one from TASK-146, at `%TEMP%\nvimos-ops\merge.<repo>.<branch>`, detached
at the old base. Add is the git step that marks a conflicted file as resolved. The commit in that
worktree makes the merge commit, which is the point where the merge stops being pending.
### The marker check
# refuse the add when the file still has a conflict marker at the start of a line
The check runs before every add, and the first matching line is reported with the file name. It reads
the file as it is in the merge worktree, so an edit made in nvim is seen.
### Moving main
git update-ref refs/heads/main <merge-sha> <old-main>
The update uses the old value as a guard: if `main` has moved since the merge started, the update
fails and nothing is lost, and Ops asks me to merge again. This is the step from TASK-146 and the
merge-beside-checkout proposal, repeated here because the verify step runs just before it.
Versions: `merge-tree --write-tree` needs git 2.38 or newer (checked: 2.46.2 here). The marker check
is a plain pattern match, and it should be tested on files with CRLF line endings, which Windows
writes.
## Open questions
Whether the merge commit should land directly on `main`, or first on the branch being merged, is the
open point. If a resolution is wrong, `main` is broken as soon as the commit lands, which is the
concern I raised. The alternative of an extra commit on `feature/api-integration`, so the resolution
can be reviewed on the pull request first, costs one more step and a commit that is not on `main`.
The other alternative is to produce the resolution as a diff, apply it to the branch, and leave
`main` untouched until the result is known to be clean. That keeps `main` safe and costs the most
work. For now the outcome is a merge on `main`, and both alternatives are written in PLAN.md.
Where the resolution happens is also worth a note. The earlier idea was to run the merge with
`--no-commit` in the main checkout, which would leave the conflict markers in the folder I work in.
The merge-beside-checkout proposal decided against that, so this change follows the merge worktree.
If that decision is reversed, the verify and add guards still apply, but the main checkout would
see markers while the merge is open.
## Decisions
- Entry: the conflict view opens automatically when the pre-flight finds a conflict. There is no key
and no entry in the rail.
- Mode: a third diff mode, beside unified and side-by-side.
- Resolve: per hunk, either side, modeled on Meld. nvim opens the conflicted file, not in diff mode.
- Add: refuses a file that still has conflict markers.
- Finish: the commit completes the merge on the base branch, after the verify step.
- No confirm dialog on Merge (decided 2026-11-15).
- Resolve re-runs the pre-flight before it opens the view.
## Impact
The conflict view is a third diff mode in `lib/ui/`, and the pre-flight and the resolve step sit in
`lib/state/pr.dart`. `lib/backend/backend.dart` gets the `merge-tree` call and the marker check. PLAN.md
already has the merge rules, the conflict view and the credit to Meld. The plain merge without a
conflict is unchanged.
## ADDED Requirements
Draft, for discussion; nothing here is decided.
### Requirement: A conflict opens the conflict view
A merge whose pre-flight finds conflicts SHALL open the conflict view and SHALL NOT run the merge.
#### Scenario: Conflict found by the pre-flight
- **WHEN** the user clicks Merge and `git merge-tree --write-tree` reports conflicted files
- **THEN** the conflict view opens listing those files, base has not moved, and the main checkout is unchanged
#### Scenario: Clean pre-flight
- **WHEN** the pre-flight reports no conflict
- **THEN** the merge runs as a plain merge, with no view
### Requirement: Pick either side per hunk
The conflict view SHALL let the user pick ours or theirs for each conflict hunk of a file.
#### Scenario: Pick a hunk
- **WHEN** the user picks theirs for a hunk
- **THEN** the file's preview shows theirs for that hunk and the other hunks are unchanged
### Requirement: Open a conflicted file in nvim
The conflict view SHALL open the conflicted file in a new nvim-qt instance, not in diff mode.
#### Scenario: Open in nvim
- **WHEN** the user chooses to open a conflicted file in nvim
- **THEN** nvim-qt starts a new instance on that file
### Requirement: Add refuses a file with conflict markers
Add SHALL refuse a file that has a conflict marker at the start of a line.
#### Scenario: File still has markers
- **WHEN** the user adds a file containing a line starting with `<<<<<<<`, `=======` or `>>>>>>>`
- **THEN** Ops refuses, names the file and the first marker line, and the file stays unresolved
### Requirement: The verify step before the commit
The commit that completes the merge SHALL run a verify step first.
#### Scenario: Verify passes
- **WHEN** no unmerged paths remain and no staged file has a marker
- **THEN** the commit completes the merge on base
#### Scenario: Verify fails
- **WHEN** an unmerged path or a marker remains
- **THEN** the commit is refused, the files are named, and base has not moved
### Requirement: Re-check on Resolve
Resolve SHALL run the pre-flight again before it opens the view.
#### Scenario: Conflict gone since the dialog
- **WHEN** base or head moved after the pre-flight and the conflict no longer exists
- **THEN** the merge runs as a plain merge and the view says so
# Add and Ignore: show every tracked file too
Tags: ops, ui
Status: In progress, for TASK-208.
## Why
Add and Ignore lists what git has something to say about: conflicts, staged, changed and untracked
files. With the preview beside it, it is also the quickest way to look through a repository's
files, except that only the changed ones are in the list. Browsing the rest means another tool.
This stretches the mode beyond its git-and-ignore purpose, knowingly: the use is worth it.
## The idea
- A toggle button in the list's header, left of the preview, ignore panes and reload buttons, and a
key (`T`), shows **all files**: every file git tracks, not only the changed and untracked ones.
- The clean tracked files come in their own section, **Tracked**, under the others; a changed file
stays in its own section and is not listed twice.
- A tracked row has the same tools as any tracked row: untrack (`−`), the eye that ignores and
untracks it, Open and Delete in the right-click menu. It has no add button (there is nothing to
stage).
- The preview, the filter and the selection work over the larger list unchanged: filter by name,
highlight, read the file beside it.
- The choice is remembered. The button is lit while all files show.
## Use cases
- I want to read `lib/state/session.dart` without opening an editor. I press `T`, type `session` in
the filter, and the preview shows it.
- I want to stop tracking a generated file that was committed by mistake. With all files shown, I
find it in Tracked and press the eye: it is ignored and untracked in one step.
- I turn it off again, and the list is back to what needs my attention.
## Technical
- The tracked paths come from `git ls-files -z` (`Repo.trackedFiles`), through the repository the
mode already opens for ignore and delete (`ensureRepo`, also when connected to Neovim).
- Proportional work: the list is read once when the toggle goes on and again after each status
refresh (git hints, an action), and replaced only when it changed, so the rows cache (keyed on the
identity of the status, the tracked list and the toggle) survives cursor moves and unchanged
refreshes. Off, no `ls-files` runs.
- `AddIgnoreSection.tracked`, after `untracked`; a tracked row is a `StatusFile` with no flags; its
letter is blank with a tooltip that says it is tracked and unchanged.
- A big repository gives a long list: the list is built lazily (`ListView.builder`), the rows are
sorted once per change.

- [x] 2 `AddIgnoreState.showTracked`: the Tracked section, read on toggle and after each refresh,
replaced only when changed; remembered in `Prefs` (`addIgnoreAllFiles`)
- [x] 3 the toggle button left of the preview button (tooltip, lit while on) and the key `T`
- [x] 4 tracked rows: untrack and the eye, no add; a muted `·` letter with a tooltip
- [x] 5 tests: the section shows and hides, no duplicates, a cursor move keeps the rows, a refresh
with the same files keeps them, a real repo's `ls-files`
- [x] 6 `PLAN.md`, Help, the Keys table
- [ ] 7 try it in the app on a big repository (thousands of files): the toggle and a refresh stay quick

# AsciiDoc in the preview, like markdown
Tags: ops, ui
Status: Proposed, for TASK-207. Not started.
## Why
Some repos write their docs in AsciiDoc (`.adoc`, `.asciidoc`) instead of markdown. The preview
renders markdown and HTML (`ops-markdown-preview`) but shows AsciiDoc as raw text.
## The idea
- An AsciiDoc file in the preview is rendered, exactly like a markdown file: the same Rendered /
Text switch, the same remembered choice, selectable text.
- Links work the same: another AsciiDoc, markdown or HTML file shows in the preview, with the
mouse's back and forward buttons; a web link goes to the browser; `xref:` and `<<id>>` cross
references to another file open it, an anchor in the same file does nothing.
- A build option like the others: `make configure asciidoc=on|off`.
## Use cases
- I highlight `docs/manual.adoc`. The preview shows its title, sections, lists, admonitions
(NOTE, TIP, WARNING) and source blocks.
- I click `xref:install.adoc[Install]`. The preview shows `install.adoc`; back returns.
## Technical
- There is no mature AsciiDoc renderer for Flutter. Options:
- convert AsciiDoc to HTML in Dart and draw it with the HTML renderer the preview already has
(`ops_html`). An AsciiDoc-to-HTML package on pub.dev, if one covers the common subset (sections,
lists, tables, source blocks, admonitions, includes off); else a small converter of our own for
that subset
- call `asciidoctor` when it is installed (Ruby or the JS build): full fidelity, but an outside
tool, slow to start, not on most Windows machines
- recommended: the Dart conversion for the common subset, drawn by `ops_html`; nothing native
- Fit with what exists
- `DocKind.asciidoc` and `.adoc` / `.asciidoc` in `DocumentAdapter.kindOf`; the switch and the
pref (`previewRendered`) already cover every document kind
- links: the converter turns `xref:` and `<<file#id>>` into `<a href>`; `resolveLink` and the
back / forward trail take them as they are
- `include::` directives are not followed (they read other files; the preview reads one)
- Effort: about a day with a usable package, two or three with our own converter for the subset.

- [ ] 1 look for an AsciiDoc-to-HTML package in Dart; try it on a few real `.adoc` files
- [ ] 2 `packages/ops_asciidoc_on` / `_off` (the converter, drawn with `ops_html`);
`make configure asciidoc=on|off`
- [ ] 3 `DocKind.asciidoc`; `.adoc` and `.asciidoc` render like markdown, with the same switch
- [ ] 4 links: `xref:` and `<<file#id>>` open in the preview with back / forward; web links go out
