# the back button and the automatic open
Status: Draft, for later. The current behavior (keep the entry) is what the app does now; this
proposal records the argument and the alternatives, not a decision to change it.
## Why
When Ops connects to a repository, `_openProject` asks the backend what the project is for and
shows the first mode with something to do: Pull request when there is a branch, else Changes when
the checkout is dirty, else Tasks. That call goes through `_setMode`, which is also the place where
a mode switch records where the user came from. So the automatic open leaves a place on the back
stack: pressing the mouse's back button right after launch returns to the mode that was shown
before the auto-open — in practice the top/start mode, Pull request.
Is that right? The user did not click anything to make that jump, so the entry is not a place they
navigate back to in the browser sense. On the other hand, the auto-open *does* replace what is on
screen, and the back button is described as "the previous place", not "the previous click". The
current decision is to keep it: back undoes the automatic jump and returns to the start mode. This
proposal is a place to decide whether that stays.
## What happens today
- The shell starts on Pull request (`_mode = Mode.pullRequest`), so the startup place is Pull
request unless the saved rail hides it, in which case the shell shows the nearest visible mode.
- On connect, a post-frame callback calls `_openProject`. `_dirs.openingTarget()` answers Pull
request, Changes or Tasks.
- `_openProject` calls `_setMode(target)` with the default `record: true`. The previous mode is
pushed as `Back to <label>`; the target mode is shown.
- If the target is already the shown mode, `_setMode` records nothing. Back then has no entry from
the auto-open.
- Pressing the back button pops that place and calls `_setMode(previous, record: false)`. The
current behavior with a hidden previous mode is to show it: hiding means "off the rail", not
"cannot be shown" (see PLAN.md, Back).
- The auto-open also happens once per backend generation (`_openedProject`), so a reconnect can
add another entry. A project opened from Repos goes through the same `_openProject` and records
a place too, but that one is a user action.
## The argument for keeping it
- **Back means "the previous place", not "the previous click".** The auto-open changed the place;
undo returns to where the app was before it. A browser also keeps the page it started on, even if
the session opened it for you.
- **It gives the app a home.** After the automatic open, one press of the back button is always
"the top of the app". That is easy to explain and easy to reach when the project opened into
Changes or Tasks and the user wanted the start mode.
- **One rule, one code path.** The alternative is a special case inside `_openProject`; the current
behavior is what every `_setMode` does. A single rule is easier to keep correct as more jumps
are added.
- **The history is already shallow at launch.** The auto-open entry is the oldest; the 50-place
cap cannot push anything important out at startup.
## The argument against
- The user made no choice, so a back button that "undoes launch" can feel wrong: on a fresh start,
back should arguably do nothing until the user navigates.
- The label is odd. The debug bar would say `Back: Back to Pull request` while the user has not
been anywhere; "Back to Connect" might describe the mental model better, but the Connect screen
is not a mode.
- If the auto-open lands on Pull request (already the start mode), nothing is recorded; the
behavior then differs depending on what the project contains. That is consistent with "no
change, no place", but it makes the first back press unpredictable from the user's seat.
- A user who connects, is auto-opened into Changes, and presses back lands in Pull request, not on
the Connect screen. If their intent was "leave this project", back is the wrong affordance and
the result may surprise them.
## Options
1. **Keep it (current).** The auto-open records a place; back returns to the start/top mode. Add a
shell test and a sentence in PLAN.md. This is the current decision.
2. **Do not record the automatic open.** `_openProject` gets a `record` flag; the connect path
passes `false`, a Repos click keeps `true`. Back after launch does nothing until the user
navigates. The code becomes one special case, but the user model is cleaner.
3. **Record only when the auto-open actually moves the user.** Already true: if the target is the
shown mode, nothing is recorded. This is an invariant to state, not a separate option.
4. **A separate "home" place.** Back after launch goes to a synthetic Start place (Pull request),
not to a history entry. This is the current observable behavior but with a different stack:
home is always there, and the auto-open is not an entry. It would also let a future "Home"
button reuse the place. More code for the same first-press result.
5. **Clear the history on connect/project open.** A fresh project starts with no back places; a
task link after the open is the first. This matches "a project is a context"; it also means the
auto-open can never be undone, which is arguably best if the user picked the project. The
downside: the history is also cleared for an automatic reconnect in the same project, losing
useful task-link places.
6. **Record the Connect screen as a place.** Back would leave the project and return to the
connect screen. That is a bigger product question: does back navigate between projects? It
would need a "disconnect" restore and a different label. Not recommended without a separate
proposal.
## Edge cases to settle if this changes
- **A hidden start mode.** With a saved rail that hides Pull request, the startup mode is the
nearest visible one (Changes). The history label must name the mode actually shown, not Pull
request.
- **The target equals the start mode.** No entry; back does nothing. Keep this, and say so in the
test.
- **Reconnects.** `_openedProject` resets for a new backend generation, so a reconnect can
auto-open again and add another entry. Is that a new place or a refresh of the same one? A
dedupe (skip if the top place has the same label and restore) may be wanted.
- **User-opened project after an automatic one.** Two entries with the same label; back walks
through both, which is correct but noisy. The debug bar makes it visible.
- **A user-opened project that lands in the shown mode.** No entry, same as the auto-open.
- **A hidden previous mode.** The current decision is to show it; a back restore must not silently
switch to a different mode.
- **Alt+[ / Alt+] and the wheel.** They are steps, not places, and do not record. Back after
stepping returns to the last recorded place, not the previous step. This is deliberate and
documented in PLAN.md.
- **The debug bar.** If the label is shown, it should read `Back: Back to Pull request` or
`Back: none`; the auto-open entry should not look like a user action. A future refinement could
label it `Back to the start` or `Back to <mode>` without changing the restore.
- **Task links and reviews.** They push entries above the auto-open. Back from a task link returns
to the auto-opened mode; a second back returns to the start mode. That is the history working as
a stack, not a special case.
- **Dialogs and context menus.** They are routes above the shell; the back button should not pop
the history while a modal is open. The root listener is below the overlay, so it does not.
## Tests this would need
- A shell test with a fake `openingTarget` and no Neovim: connect in a dirty checkout, assert the
auto-open shows Changes, press `kBackMouseButton`, assert Pull request and the rail selection.
- The same with Pull request hidden in the saved rail: the start place is the nearest visible
mode, not Pull request.
- The target already shown: back does nothing.
- A user-opened project from Repos: back returns to the mode that was shown before the click.
- The debug bar line: `Back: none` before any jump, the label after a jump, `none` after the
stack is exhausted.
- An auto-open followed by a task link and a review: back walks review → task → auto-open target
→ start mode.
## Recommendation
Keep the current behavior for now. It is one rule, it gives a predictable first back press, and it
matches the "previous place" wording. Revisit only if the back button starts reading as "undo the
project I chose": then option 2 (do not record the automatic open) is the smallest change, and
option 5 (clear on connect) is the stronger statement. Whatever is chosen, record it in PLAN.md and
cover the hidden-start-mode and target-equals-start cases with tests.
# a resize costs only what moves
Tags: performance
Status: In Progress, for TASK-198.
## Why
Add and Ignore's side pane got this pass in TASK-191 (`215a61a`). The edge anchors on the pointer's
x at drag start, so no delta is lost between frames; the width goes through a `ValueNotifier`
that only the pane listens to, so the list and the preview are relaid but never rebuilt; and the
content widget stays the same instance on every frame of the drag.
The other resizes have not had it. Help rebuilt every key group, table and highlighted span on
each width change; that part is fixed (the split and the column tree are cached by column count
and query), but the remaining cost is text layout: a hundred wrapped descriptions lay out again at
every new width, 80-220 ms per frame in a widget test. The shell's `IndexedStack` also lays out all
nine modes on every window resize, though only one is on screen. The Pull request and Changes left
panes (`ResizablePane`) still add `details.delta` to the width of the last build and `setState` on
every pointer event.
## The idea
For every drag-to-resize and every layout the window drives:
- anchor the drag on the pointer (start size and start x), not on the last built size
- one listener, at the widget that sizes; the neighbours and the content keep their widget
instances and are relaid, not rebuilt
- a window resize is a special case: keep the last laid-out content, scale it while the width
moves, and reflow once the window has been still for a moment
- a hidden mode or pane is not laid out at all; it keeps its state and scroll, and lays out when
it is shown again
## Help: the decisions
- **Freeze and reflow.** A width change keeps the last laid-out table. The table reflows once,
**150 ms** after the last width change (a window drag has no reliable end event).
- **Uniform scale.** While frozen, the table scales on both axes to the new width, so text is
briefly smaller or larger but never stretched.
- **One line while resizing.** During the frozen state the descriptions are a single line with an
ellipsis; normal wrapping returns with the reflow. This costs one rebuild at the start of the
drag and one at the end, not one per frame.
- **360 px columns, 250 px floor.** The current look stays. No column-width setting. A column is
never narrower than **250 px**, during the drag or at rest; below that the right edge is clipped
(no horizontal scrollbar).
- `UiTiming` span `help.resize` times a width change to the painted frame.
## Hidden modes and panes
- Replace the shell's `IndexedStack` with a keep-alive stack: every mode's element and render
object stay alive, so selection and scroll survive, but only the shown child is laid out and
painted. A hidden mode never lays out on a window resize; it lays out once when shown.
- A child that was never laid out gets one layout the first time it is hidden (so it has a size);
after that it waits.
- The same primitive applies to panes that are hidden inside a mode and still built.
- This is the layout side of `ops-hidden-panes-idle`, which stops hidden states from doing I/O.
- **Tried and reverted 2026-11-20.** The first version laid out a hidden child once and then never
again. A hidden mode that changed (a load, a notice) stayed dirty; the semantics pass then threw
`!semantics.parentDataDirty` and `!childSemantics.renderObject._needsLayout` every frame, and the
live log filled with thousands of assertions. It also delayed layout-built content (a filter
field) by a frame on a mode switch. The app is back on `IndexedStack`. A retry needs a dirty
hidden subtree to lay itself out (a relayout boundary was not enough in practice) or to leave
the render tree without losing its state.
## Technical notes
- Help: `_columns` ran inside `LayoutBuilder` and built new `_KeyColumn`s, `Table`s and
`Text.rich` spans every time. The split is cached by column count and the column tree by
(count, query). The new freeze keeps that tree and applies a uniform `Transform.scale`; a
`Timer` (150 ms) ends the resize and rebuilds at the final width.
- The 250 px floor means the laid-out content width is
`max(available, count * 250 + padding)`; the view clips rather than shrinking a column.
- `ResizablePane`: replace `d.delta.dx` with the anchor (the side pane already does this).
- Keep-alive stack: a `MultiChildRenderObjectWidget` over a `RenderBox` with
`ContainerRenderObjectMixin`; `performLayout` lays out the shown child, and the first time
each hidden child; `paint` and `hitTestChildren` use only the shown child. `ExcludeSemantics`
stays as it is. Reverted: see the note above; the child must never stay dirty.
- Tests: Help keeps the same `RichText` instances on a drag frame and reflows after 150 ms; a
column is at least 250 px and the overflow clips. The keep-alive stack tests are removed with
the implementation.
# Tasks
## 1. Build
- [x] 1.1 Help: cache the split by column count and the column tree by (count, query), so a
width change in the same structure lays out and does not rebuild the key rows
- [x] 1.2 Help: a `UiTiming` span (`help.resize`), and the rule in CLAUDE.md and PLAN.md
- [x] 1.3 Help: freeze the table on a width change; scale it uniformly to the new width; reflow
150 ms after the last change; one-line descriptions while resizing, wrapping at rest
- [x] 1.4 Help: 360 px columns, a 250 px floor, and clip the right edge below it (no setting)
- [ ] 1.5 keep-alive stack in the shell: hidden modes keep state and scroll but are not laid out.
**Tried and reverted 2026-11-20**: a hidden mode that changed (a load, a notice) was left dirty,

`!childSemantics.renderObject._needsLayout` in a storm; it also changed when layout-built content
(a filter field) appeared on a mode switch. Needs a design where a dirty hidden subtree lays

# the commit message as a dialog from any mode
Tags: ops, ui
Status: Proposed, for TASK-209. Not started; an idea to try, not a settled design.
## Why
The commit message lives in Changes: its field under the file lists, and a large dialog
(`CommitMessageDialog`) opened from there. Staging often happens elsewhere (Add and Ignore, the
Pull request view, Neovim), and writing the message means switching to Changes first. A message
started and left half done is easy to lose.
Whether a modal is the right shape is an open question; the proposal is to try it.
## The idea
- One key, from any mode, brings up the commit message as a dialog over the app, like a dialog on a
web page: the app dims behind it.
- Inside, a text area about 90 characters wide and 6 lines tall by default, with room around it; it
can be resized (a grip at its lower right corner), and the dialog grows with it.
- Three buttons at the bottom:
- **Accept**: commit with the message; the dialog closes and the draft is cleared
- **Hide**: close and keep the text; it is there again the next time the dialog comes up
- **Cancel**: close and throw the text away
- An **X** in the upper right corner, **Esc**, and a click outside the dialog also close it. They
keep the text, like Hide, so nothing typed is lost by a stray click or key (to be confirmed: the
alternative is that they act like Cancel).
- The draft is one: the same text as the commit field in Changes, so starting in one and finishing
in the other works.
## Use cases
- I stage two files in Add and Ignore, press the key, write `add-ignore: all files toggle` and the

# How the lost commit keys were found
Notes for the next bug of this kind: what was tried, what each step showed, and why the obvious
suspect was not it.
## 1. The report
Alt+] to Changes, stage a file with "add", `cc` to the commit field, type a burst: only the first
letter stayed in the field.
## 2. Tests that did not reproduce it
Widget tests replayed the steps: the Changes view alone, then the whole shell on a real local
repository with the file watcher running, with a click on the field and with `cc`, and with the
refresh after the stage landing in the middle of the burst. In every run the keyboard stayed in the
field, no key handler claimed a letter, and the text input connection opened once.
So the cause was in what the tests don't have: the real Windows engine, real timing, the real
accessibility layer.
## 3. A trace in the running app
A temporary trace in `changes_view.dart` wrote `[commit-trace]` lines to `out/live.log`: every key
with its character and the focused node, every change of the field's text, every focus change of
the field. One run showed:
50596 ms  key down C            pending=true    (cc completes)
50597 ms  field focus=true
51002 ms  key down H  char=h    focus=commit message
51007 ms  text "h"
51056 ms  field focus=false                     (49 ms after the first letter)
51112 ms  key down K  char=e    focus=_ModalScopeState Focus Scope
The first letter landed. About one frame later the field lost the keyboard to the page's
top-level focus scope, and the following keys went nowhere.
## 4. The navigation-key question
The first idea was the rule that makes an arrow key at the edge of the commit field step out of
it (Left to the rail, Up to the list above), with H being Left in hjkl, and the same for the other
direction letters `j k l` and `w a s d`. An exception for those letters in the field seemed to be
the fix.
It wasn't the cause:
- the rule only looks at the real arrow keys (`final nav = arrow ? navKey(e) : null; // letters
type into the field` in `CommitBox`), so a letter never reaches it
- a key handler moves the focus within a millisecond of the key: after `cc` the field had the
keyboard 1 ms after the second `c`; here the focus left 54 ms after the `h` went down, a frame
later, not on the key
- the Left rule sends the keyboard to the rail, and the trace would have said `focus=rail`; it said
the page's focus scope, which is where focus falls when a node is unfocused
- the `h` itself landed as text (`text "h"`), so it was typing, not a command
The letters do belong in the field, so the suggestion became a test that pins it: `h j k l w a s d`
(including the D-position key the layout reads as Right) type into the empty field and keep the
keyboard there, and only the arrows step out.
## 5. Who called unfocus
The trace's focus node (`_TracedFocusNode`) printed a stack trace whenever `unfocus()` was called on
it. The next run named the caller:
_TracedFocusNode.unfocus
_TextFieldState.build.<closure>            (material_ui text_field.dart: handleDidLoseAccessibilityFocus)
SemanticsAnnotationsMixin._performDidLoseAccessibilityFocus
SemanticsOwner.performAction
FlutterView.updateSemantics … PipelineOwner.flushSemantics … drawFrame
Not app code and not a key: the accessibility bridge, while the frame sent its semantics update.
## 6. Why the bridge thought the focus moved
In the engine, the Windows bridge takes the node flagged focused as its focus and, when that node
changes, sends the previous one "lost accessibility focus". A widget test running as Windows listed
the focused nodes in the shell:
after cc:       #55 textField=true label="Commit message  (cc, Ctrl+Enter commits)" value=""
after h:        #55 …                                                               value="h"
a frame later:  #74 textField=true label=""                                          value="h"
The field's focused node changed from #55 to #74 one frame after the first letter. Narrowed down
with plain text fields:
- a field with only a hint: the node stays
- a field with a fixed suffix of two buttons: the node stays
- a field whose suffix gains a button with the text (the X): a new node
- the same growing suffix inside `Semantics(container: true)`: the node stays
## 7. The fix and its check
`Semantics(container: true)` around the commit field's buttons and around `ClearButton`. A test
running as Windows types the first letter and expects the same focused node and the keyboard still
in the field; it fails without the fix.
## What to take from it
- When tests can't reproduce a focus bug, trace it in the running app: keys, text, focus changes,
and a stack trace on `unfocus`.
- On Windows, a text field's focus is tied to its semantics node. Anything that reshapes that node
while you type (a button that appears inside the field) can unfocus it, but only while the
accessibility layer is active, so it may never show on another machine.
# the commit field keeps the keyboard while you type
Tags: bug, accessibility, keys
Status: Approved, for TASK-211. The fix is in and verified in the running app (2026-11-23).
## Why
In Changes, `cc` puts the keyboard in the commit message field. Typing a burst there, like the first
letters of a summary, kept only the first letter: the rest went nowhere. The field had lost the
keyboard after one character, and the later keys reached no widget at all.
It made the commit field unusable for anyone who types quickly, which is everyone writing a commit
message.
## The cause
The field's buttons on the right, inside the field, are the large-window button and an X that
clears the message. The X only exists while there is text, so the first letter adds it. Adding it
reshapes the field's semantics: the editable text moves into a new semantics node, with a new id,
and that node carries the "focused" flag.
The Windows accessibility bridge in the Flutter engine (`accessibility_bridge.cc`) follows the
focused flag. When the focused node changes, it tells the node it had before that it "lost
accessibility focus" (`SetLastFocusedId`). The old node still belongs to the text field, and a
Material `TextField` on Windows unfocuses itself when it loses accessibility focus
(`handleDidLoseAccessibilityFocus` in `text_field.dart`). So the first frame after the first letter
took the keyboard away.
It only happens while Windows accessibility is active for the app, which is also why the
`Failed to update ui::AXTree` errors show up at all (change `ops-tooltip-semantics`). Something on
this machine keeps it active.
## The fix
The buttons in a field are one semantics node of their own, `Semantics(container: true)` around
them. The X can come and go inside it without touching the field's node, so the focused node keeps
its id and the bridge has nothing to report.
- the commit field's buttons (`_FieldButtons`, `lib/ui/changes_view.dart`)
- the shared X of the filter and picker fields (`ClearButton`, `lib/ui/widgets.dart`); every
other text field with an X uses it (Add and Ignore, Directories, Help, the rev pickers, the Tasks
filter, the command palette)
## How it was found
The steps, the dead ends and the navigation-key question are in [debugging.md](debugging.md).
The technique that found it, a temporary trace in the running app, with the code to add it again,
is in [trace-technique.md](trace-technique.md).
## Technical notes
- `test/support/semantics_focus.dart`: `focusedSemanticsIds` lists the nodes flagged focused,
`expectStableFocusWhileTyping` types the first letter and expects the same focused node and the
keyboard still in the field. Tests that use it run as Windows
(`TargetPlatformVariant.only(TargetPlatform.windows)`); only there does the text field have the
unfocus handler.
- `commit_message_test.dart` "the first letter keeps the keyboard in the field": fails without the
fix, passes with it.
- `widgets_test.dart` "a filter field keeps the keyboard when its x appears": a guard; a plain
field with only the `ClearButton` kept its node even before the fix, but any button added next
to the X would bring the problem back.
- `commit_message_test.dart` "hjkl and wasd type into the empty field": pins that the navigation
letters type and only the arrows step out (see debugging.md).
- The temporary commit trace in `changes_view.dart` (`[commit-trace]` lines in `out/live.log`,
`_TracedFocusNode`) confirmed the fix in a `make live` run and is removed.
- Upstream: a Flutter issue is worth filing. The bridge sending "lost accessibility focus" when a
node's own semantics are split is a framework or engine bug, and a text field that unfocuses
on it turns an accessibility detail into lost typing.

# The technique: a temporary trace in the running app
How the lost commit keys were tracked down once tests could not reproduce them, written so it can be
done again for the next bug of this kind: keys, text or focus that behave differently in `make live`
than in a widget test.
## When to reach for it
- widget tests replay the steps and the bug doesn't show
- the bug lives in what tests replace with fakes: the Windows engine, real timing, the accessibility
layer, the IME, the mouse resting somewhere
- guessing would mean changing code without knowing which change matters
A trace turns "something takes the keyboard" into a timeline you can read, one run of the real
steps at a time.
## The idea
Four questions, each answered by one probe that writes a line to `out/live.log`:
| question                                | probe                                                         |
| did the key reach the app, and where?   | a `HardwareKeyboard` handler that logs every key down         |
| did the text arrive?                    | a listener on the field's `TextEditingController`             |
| when did the field gain or lose focus?  | a listener on the field's `FocusNode`                         |
| who took the focus?                     | a `FocusNode` subclass that prints a stack trace on `unfocus` |
Every line carries the milliseconds since the view started and a fixed tag (`[commit-trace]`), so
`grep` picks them out of the log and the times can be compared. The gaps matter: a key handler
moves focus within a millisecond of its key, while a frame is about 16-50 ms; a change that comes
one frame after a key is the frame's doing, not the key's.
## How to add it
In the view's `State`, debug builds only (`kDebugMode`), so it can never ship:
```dart
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart' show kDebugMode;
// TEMPORARY (<date>): trace of <field>, to find <symptom>. Remove once found.
final _messageFocus = kDebugMode ? _TracedFocusNode(debugLabel: 'commit message') : FocusNode(debugLabel: 'commit message');
final _traceClock = Stopwatch()..start();
void _trace(String what) => debugPrint('[commit-trace] ${_traceClock.elapsedMilliseconds.toString().padLeft(7)} ms  $what');
bool _traceKey(KeyEvent e) {
if (e is KeyDownEvent || e is KeyRepeatEvent) {
final focus = FocusManager.instance.primaryFocus?.debugLabel ?? '${FocusManager.instance.primaryFocus}';
_trace('key ${e.logicalKey.keyLabel} char=${e.character} focus=$focus');
return false; // never claims the key: the app still sees it
@override
void initState() {
super.initState();
if (kDebugMode) {
HardwareKeyboard.instance.addHandler(_traceKey);
_message.addListener(() => _trace('text "${_message.text}" sel=${_message.selection.baseOffset}'));
_messageFocus.addListener(() => _trace('field focus=${_messageFocus.hasFocus} '
'attached=${_messageFocus.context?.mounted ?? false} '
'primary=${FocusManager.instance.primaryFocus?.debugLabel}'));
@override
void dispose() {
if (kDebugMode) HardwareKeyboard.instance.removeHandler(_traceKey);
super.dispose();
And the focus node that names the caller:
```dart
/// TEMPORARY: says who takes the keyboard from the field.
class _TracedFocusNode extends FocusNode {
_TracedFocusNode({super.debugLabel});
@override
void unfocus({UnfocusDisposition disposition = UnfocusDisposition.scope}) {
if (hasFocus) debugPrint('[commit-trace] unfocus($disposition) called from:\n${StackTrace.current}');
super.unfocus(disposition: disposition);
Notes:
- the `HardwareKeyboard` handler runs before every `Focus` handler, so it sees each key even when
something else claims it; it returns `false` so it never changes what the app does
- `primaryFocus?.debugLabel` names the node that has the keyboard; give new `FocusNode`s a
`debugLabel` (the project does already, for the debug bar)
- a node is created in a field initializer, so swapping it in needs a hot restart (`R`), not a hot
reload (`r`)
- `attached` tells the two ways to lose focus apart: `unfocus()` was called (a stack trace appears)
or the field's element was rebuilt and its node detached (`attached=false`, no stack trace)
## How to run it
1. Add the probes, `make analyze`.
2. `R` in `make live`.
3. Do the steps once, as the bug happens (here: `Alt+]` to Changes, `cc`, a quick burst).
4. Read the trace:
`grep "commit-trace" out/live.log | grep -v "Alt Left"` (held Alt repeats flood it), and the
lines after `unfocus(` for the stack trace.
## Reading it, this time
Round one gave the timeline: the first letter landed, the field lost focus 49 ms later, and the next
keys found the page's focus scope. That ruled out a key command (it would have moved focus at once,
and to the rail) and pointed at something on the next frame.
Round two added the stack trace on `unfocus`. It named the caller outright: the text field's "lost
accessibility focus" handler, called by the Windows accessibility bridge while the frame sent its
semantics update. From there, a widget test running as Windows could list the focused semantics
node before and after the letter and show its id changing: a reproduction without the real
machine, and the test that now guards the fix.
The verification run used the same trace: the keyboard stayed in the field through `hello`, held
keys and backspaces, and no `unfocus` stack trace appeared.
## Taking it out
Remove the probes, the `_TracedFocusNode` class and the `kDebugMode` import in the same change as
the fix, once a run of the real steps shows the fix working. `grep -n "commit-trace\|_trace"` on the
file must come back empty.
# make configure: build options in one place
Tags: ops, build
Status: In progress, for TASK-204.
## Why
ops has one build option so far, the PDF pages, with three targets of its own (`pdf-on`, `pdf-off`,
`pdf-status`). Rendered markdown is about to become the second. A pair of targets per option doesn't
scale, and there is no single place that says how the current checkout is configured.
## The idea
- One step, `make configure`, in the spirit of `./configure` from the autotools, without autotools.
- Options are set as make variables: `make configure pdf=on markdown=off`. An option left out keeps
its current setting.
- `make configure` with no options prints how the checkout is configured, one line per option.
- The setting stays until it is changed again: every later `make live`, `make dev`, `make build` uses
it.
- Each option has a default (PDF off, markdown on); a fresh clone builds with the defaults without
running configure.
- `make release` configures what it ships first, so a release never depends on what was left
configured locally.
## Use cases
- I want to check the PDF build still compiles: `make configure pdf=on`, `make dev`, then
`make configure pdf=off` again.
- I'm not sure what this checkout builds: `make configure` prints `off pdf` and ` on markdown`.
- I run `make release` while PDF is on locally. It switches PDF off before building.
## Technical
- An option is a Dart package in two variants with the same name and API, `packages/<pkg>_on` and
`packages/<pkg>_off` (as `ops_pdf` is today). `pubspec.yaml` depends on the default variant.
- `tool/configure.ps1` writes the git-ignored `pubspec_overrides.yaml`, with a
`dependency_overrides` entry for each option that differs from its default, and runs `pub get`
when anything changed. No entries left: the file is removed. The file is the configuration; there
is no second state file to drift from it.
- The options are one table in the script (name, package, default); a new option is a line there and
its two packages.
- Output follows the scripts' style: one line per option, the state right-aligned, nothing for an
option that was already so; `-WhatIf` for a dry run.
- `pubspec.lock` is committed from the default configuration; another one shows it as modified.
- Replaces `tool/pdf.ps1` and the `pdf-on` / `pdf-off` / `pdf-status` targets.

# mark dead ignore rules
Tags: integrate-purrage
Status: Draft, for TASK-193. Follows `ops-ignore-pane`.
## Why
Some lines in a `.gitignore` can never have an effect, and nothing says so. The Ignore panes'
Flip (turn a rule into a `!` negation and back) makes it easy to write one.
How git reads the rules, in short:
- a file's rules are read top to bottom; the last rule that matches a path decides
- a `.gitignore` in a folder adds its rules for that folder and below, after the ones above it
- `!pattern` re-includes what an earlier rule excluded
- the catch: when a *folder* is excluded, git does not look inside it at all, so no rule can bring
back a file in it. `build/` followed by `!build/keep.txt` does nothing; the negation is dead. (It
works only when the folder itself is not excluded, e.g. `build/*` then `!build/keep.txt`.)
## The idea
The lines pane marks the dead lines (muted, struck through) with a tooltip saying why:
- a negation whose path lies inside a folder an earlier rule excludes, in the same file or in a
`.gitignore` above: "git never looks inside build/, so this cannot re-include anything"
- a negation that re-includes nothing because no earlier rule excludes it: "nothing above
excludes this"
- a duplicate of an earlier line in the same file: "the same rule is on line 4"
Only the shapes that can be decided with certainty are marked; a rule the check cannot decide is
left alone, never marked wrongly.
## Cost
- No git call: the check works on the rules the pane already read, in memory.
- It runs when a file is read or edited, not per frame or per cursor move: a few hundred lines at
most, cheap.
- The work is in the matching: a negation against the folder rules above it. Literal folders
(`/build/`, `build/`) are a string check; wildcards (`*/cache/`, `**/out/`) need a gitignore
pattern matcher (pure Dart, unit-tested, or reused from a package).
## Technical notes
- A pure `deadRules(fileRules, rulesAbove)` returning per line the reason or null; unit tests per
shape, including the cases it must leave alone.
- The pane asks it after each load; nothing else changes.

The dev (debug) build and the release build of ops look the same in the taskbar, the window title
and Explorer. With both running, or a release copy in `~/.local/bin` next to a fresh debug build,

- The dev build carries its own icon: the ops icon with a small wrench laid over it. The handle
comes in from the bottom-right corner; the head points toward the centre, its open jaw facing the
middle.

# hidden modes and panes stay idle
Tags: performance
Status: Draft, for TASK-192.
## Why
The shell keeps every mode built in an `IndexedStack`, so a mode keeps its state and scroll when
you come back. But "built" has come to mean "working": each state listens to the backend's git
hints and re-queries what it shows, whether it is on screen or not ("a git hint from the backend
makes each state re-query what it shows"). With nine modes, one save in Neovim can set off RPCs,
git calls and rebuilds for eight screens nobody looks at. The same holds for panes inside a mode
that a switch or a toggle hides.
It is the I/O side of the rule in CLAUDE.md, *proportional work*: an interaction, or an outside
event, costs in proportion to what it changes on screen.
## The idea
- A hidden mode or pane does no work. When an event would make it re-query, it only marks itself
stale.
- When it is shown again, a stale part refreshes once, before or right after its first frame; a
part that is not stale shows what it had, with no call at all.
- What stays live while hidden is named, with a reason: the status store (shared by Changes and
Add and Ignore, and the source of the badges), the jobs, the connection, anything the rail or
the status bar shows.
- The ignore and preview panes of Add and Ignore are the first case (change `ops-ignore-pane`);
this change carries the logic to the rest.
## Where it applies
To be checked mode by mode, applicable or not:
- Pull request: branches, commits, the diff of the selected file
- Changes: the diff of the selected file (the lists come from the shared status store)
- Add and Ignore: done in `ops-ignore-pane`

# HTML pages in a real browser engine
Tags: ops, ui
Status: Proposed, for TASK-206. Not started; only if the light renderer is not enough.
## Why
The preview draws HTML without a browser (`ops-markdown-preview`, `flutter_widget_from_html_core`):
tags and basic CSS, no JavaScript. That is right for generated docs, reports and notes. A real web
page (a built site, a coverage report with scripts, a page laid out with flexbox or grid) comes out
broken, and the Open button is the only way to see it as it is.
## The idea
- An HTML file can be shown by the real engine, the one Edge uses, inside the preview.
- It is a third view next to Rendered and Text (Browser), or it replaces Rendered for HTML when the
build has it; to be decided by trying both.
- Scripts are off by default; a local page never reaches the network unless I allow it for that page.
- A build option like PDF: `make configure webview=on`; without it the light renderer stays.
## Use cases
- I highlight `coverage/index.html`. The preview shows the report as Edge would, its tables and
colours intact.
- I highlight a page from a static site build. Its layout is right; links to other pages of the site
open in the preview as they do today.
## Technical
- Windows 11 ships the engine: WebView2 (Edge, Chromium). Nothing large is bundled; the
`webview_windows` package (or `flutter_inappwebview`'s Windows support) wraps it.
- What makes it a few days, not one:
- it is a native view drawn into a texture: it needs a fixed height, while the preview is a list
of several files one under the other. Likely: a browser view only when a single HTML file is
highlighted, filling the pane
- keys and focus: the view takes the keyboard while focused, so the app's keys (pane motion,
Alt+1..9) need a way out (Esc, or the shell's keys handled before it)
- overlays: tooltips and menus over the view, and the text is not part of the app's selection
- security: JavaScript off unless allowed, no network for `file:` pages, no downloads
- the runtime: present on Windows 11; the stub shows the light renderer when it is missing
- navigation inside the view: links handled by the app's history (back / forward), not by the
view's own
- Like PDF, the build is slow to try and needs a test that builds it in CI before a release ships
it on.
# Tasks
- [ ] 1 try `webview_windows` in a scratch build: a local page, scripts off, no network
- [ ] 2 decide the place: a third view (Browser) or Rendered for HTML; one file filling the pane
- [ ] 3 `packages/ops_webview_on` / `_off`, `make configure webview=on|off`
- [ ] 4 keys and focus: a way back to the app's keys; Esc leaves the view
- [ ] 5 links through the app's history (back / forward), not the view's
- [ ] 6 a CI build with it on before a release turns it on
# the Ignore panes, closer to Purrage's
Tags: integrate-purrage
Status: In Progress, for TASK-191; the decisions are settled (see Decisions).
## Why
The Add and Ignore mode's Ignore pane (`p`) was ported from Purrage in a hurry and lost its shape.
Purrage showed every `.gitignore` of the project in a list, with the selected file's lines next to
it; Ops shows only the files around the cursor row, stacked in one column, and reads them again
after every cursor rest.
Both apps also carry a feature that can never show anything: the pane asks git which rule ignores
the row under the cursor (`git check-ignore -v`). Every row of the list is either untracked and
*not* ignored (git status would not list it otherwise) or tracked, and without `--no-index`
`check-ignore` never reports a tracked file. So the answer is always "no match". The test that
covers it (`test/ignore_test.dart`, "the pane shows the ignore files of the cursor row and moves
with the cursor") only passes because its fake lookup invents a match the app cannot produce. The
Ignore dialog has the same dead branch ("already ignored by … in file:line").
The deeper problem is the question itself. The cursor can only rest on a row the list shows, and
the list shows exactly the paths git did not ignore; an ignored untracked path is absent. A tracked
path can match a `.gitignore` pattern, but ignore rules do not apply to tracked files, and
`check-ignore` does not report one without `--no-index`. So "which rule ignores this row" has no
reachable answer: the pane asks why a visible row is ignored, about rows that are not ignored.
## The idea
Bring back Purrage's two panes, without the match lookup, and keep what Ops added.
The value is the ignore surface itself — seeing where the ignore files are and editing their rules
— not a verdict about the highlighted row. Purrage's two panes keep that value with the match
removed; there, the match is only a shortcut for choosing which file to show. Ops made it the
pane, so removing it leaves a path-scoped list with a gap where the reason for the pane used to be.
- Two panes side by side
- left: the list of every `.gitignore` in the project, named by its folder; the top-most one is
the "project .gitignore" (not "root"); 35 % of the pane's width, at least 80 px
- right: every line of the selected `.gitignore` as it is, comments and blank lines too, without
line numbers; the rest of the width, for the rules
- No `.git/info/exclude` and no global ignore file in the list: `.gitignore` files only.
- The list does not follow the cursor row: it starts on the project `.gitignore` when it exists,
else the first file found, and keeps the file the user picked last for the session.
- No "which rule matches" verdict, no highlighted rule, no `check-ignore` per cursor rest.
- The files are read once when the panes open, and again only when the status reports a changed
`.gitignore` path or after the app's own write; moving the cursor in the file list reads nothing
(proportional work: a cursor move moves a highlight).
- Line actions, on every line (rules, comments and blank lines, so any line can be deleted)
- the right-click menu: Delete, Dirname, Flip, Open
- Dirname takes a rule one folder up, as in Purrage: disabled where there is no folder above
(the tooltip says why), never a wildcard-only parent (`**/`, which matches everything below),
and only removes the line when the parent rule is already in the file
- not a rule (a comment or a blank line): not enabled; "dirname only works on positive rules"
- a negation: not enabled; "please edit negation rules manually"
- a wildcard-only parent: not enabled; "please edit wildcard rules manually"
- no folder above (`*.log`, `/x.log`, `build/`): not enabled; "no folder above this rule"
- Flip toggles the leading `!` on a rule, so a positive rule becomes a negation and back; it is
disabled on comments and blank lines ("flip only works on rules")
- Open opens the `.gitignore` in the editor at that line
- the hover buttons stay, an exception to the rule that ported Purrage modes have no hover-only
buttons; the "one folder up" button is renamed Dirname, the same word as in the menu
- Purrage's Open in editor (the selected `.gitignore`) and New here (a `.gitignore` in the cursor
row's folder — inside the folder for a directory row, at the root for the project file; the new
file shows up as an untracked row, tracked like anything else).
- Ignore-file I/O goes through the backend, never a local path:
- `RepoBackend` gains `loadIgnorePanes` (tracked `.gitignore` list plus the selected file's text
in one call), `untrackedIgnoreFiles` (added later), `readIgnoreFile`, `appendIgnoreLines`,
`replaceIgnoreLine`, `insertIgnoreLine`, `createIgnoreFile`, and an `IgnoreFileRef` that names
either a repo-relative `.gitignore` or the `.git/info/exclude` target
- `LocalBackend` delegates to `Repo`; `NvimBackend` calls a new relay module, so Neovim in a VM or
over SSH works
- Open in editor uses `EditorSession` (`session.editor`), not a local repository root
- after a write, the file is read again and the new rule's line is found by a helper (not by
guessing from the append result)
- Keys as in Purrage, plus Enter
- the `.gitignore` list and the lines are two Tab stops; `j` / `k` pick a file in the list and
move the line cursor; Shift+wheel scrolls the lines
- Enter opens in the editor: the selected `.gitignore` from the list, the file at the line cursor
from the lines
- After the Ignore dialog writes a rule, the list selects the `.gitignore` it went into, and the new
line is put in the middle of the lines pane at once, without an animated scroll.
- The area is shared with the preview, one at a time: a switch above it chooses the ignore panes
or the preview, as Purrage's Git lists / Preview, and is remembered.
- The area is resizable by its left edge, as in Purrage: the width is remembered, and the area is
hidden by default when the window is narrower than 600 px; `p` or the switch still opens it.
## Performance
- Not on every refresh. A refresh comes with nearly every git hint (each save in Neovim); the panes
do not read again then.
- the `.gitignore` files are found again only when the status lists a changed `.gitignore` path,
or after the app's own write
- only the selected file's text is read; the list needs names, not contents
- one `loadIgnorePanes` call answers both (the tracked list and the selected file's text), not one
call per file: over the relay every call is a round trip; `untrackedIgnoreFiles` adds the rest
after the tracked ones are on screen
- the first call also includes the project `.gitignore` when it exists but is untracked, so the
default selection and its text are there on open; the later call adds the nested untracked ones
- Nothing while hidden. With the switch on Preview, the ignore panes neither listen nor read: they
mark themselves stale and load when they are shown again. The same for the preview while the
ignore panes are shown. This round does it for these two panes only; the rest of the app is the
change `ops-hidden-panes-idle`.
- Every line has the same height (`itemExtent`), so centring a line is one `jumpTo` with no layout
pass to measure first. A line is one line, cut with an ellipsis, never wrapped. The height
follows the text style, not a constant, so it stays right when custom font sizes come.
- Discovery off the UI thread, in two steps: the tracked `.gitignore` files (`ls-files --cached`)
show at once; the untracked ones (`--others`, which walks every untracked folder and can take
seconds in a repo with an unignored `node_modules`) are added when they arrive.
## Usability
- Keys follow the motion rules of the rest of the app (CLAUDE.md, Keys)
- Right / `l` goes from the file list to the `.gitignore` list, then to the lines; Left / `h`
back the same way
- going up into a list from below lands on its lowest visible item; Ctrl+arrow jumps between
the panes
- new focus nodes get a `debugLabel` and an entry in the debug bar's `focusRoles`
- Undo: Delete, Flip and Dirname act at once; the notice after one has an Undo button. One undo at
a time: the next edit replaces it. Undo writes the old line back, with the same check that the
file did not change meanwhile.
- `Delete` on the line cursor deletes that line, with the same Undo.
- The effect of an edit is said: after the refresh that follows, a short notice counts the rows that
came back or left the list ("3 files back in the list", "2 files now ignored"), from the status
before and after, with no extra git call.
- Which files apply to the row (a trial): the `.gitignore` list marks the files that govern the
cursor row's folder, its own and those above it. It only marks; the selection stays where the
user put it. A string-prefix check per file, no git. Kept if it helps, dropped if it is noise.
- Empty: a project without any `.gitignore` shows that, with a "Create project .gitignore" button.
- Narrow: under 600 px of window width the area is hidden by default, but `p` (or the switch)
still opens it, as in Purrage. An explicit open stays open until `p` closes it; a later window
resize does not undo the user's choice.
- Open in Neovim: after a write, a `.gitignore` that is open in a Neovim buffer without unsaved
changes is reloaded there (the relay, like `:checktime` for that buffer), so Neovim shows the
change at once. A buffer with unsaved changes is left alone: the app writes the file, and
Neovim's own "changed on disk" warning is enough.
## Adjustments to Purrage
- No match lookup, no "not ignored" verdict, no Open line for a match in `exclude` or the global
file (all dead, see Why).
- The panes explain the ignore surface, not the row's ignore state: a visible row is never ignored,
and a match on a tracked row has no effect on it.
- The list does not follow the cursor row (Purrage followed the match).
- The project `.gitignore`, not `root`; `.gitignore` files only.
- Every line is shown and can be deleted, comments and blank lines too; no line numbers.
- Hover buttons on the lines, in addition to the menu; the menu also has Flip and Open.
- Enter opens in the editor; the lines have a cursor to open from.
- Ignore I/O goes through the backend, so a Neovim in a VM or over SSH is supported.
- Hidden under 600 px of window width (Purrage: 900 px).
## Cleanups that go with it
- Remove the test that invents a match (`test/ignore_test.dart`, "the pane shows the ignore files
of the cursor row and moves with the cursor") and its "one lookup per resting place" assertion;
a fake match is not a regression test for a reachable feature. Replace it with tests of what the
panes do: the list starts on the project `.gitignore` and keeps a pick across cursor moves, a
cursor move reads no file, a written rule selects its file and centres its line.
- Remove the match from the pane state (`IgnoreInfo.match`, `isMatch`, the verdict line, the
highlighted rule, the `checkIgnore` call, the debounce timer and the per-path cache).
- Remove the Ignore dialog's dead "already ignored" branch: `IgnoreChoice.already`, the
`checkIgnoreAll` call in `forSelection`, `AddIgnoreState.alreadyIgnored()`, the preview lines
and the "git already ignores it" problem.
- The Ignore dialog's target names follow the panes: "project .gitignore", not "root .gitignore".
- Ignore I/O moves off the local `Repo` and onto `RepoBackend`; `ensureRepo()` and the Neovim-root
reopen stay only for the actions that still need a local repository (delete), not for the pane.
- Unit tests for the pure helpers: every dirname rule shape and refusal (leading spaces, escaped
`\#` and `\!`, folder-only rules, bracket-only parents, `**/`), Flip on positive, negated,
escaped (`\!`), leading-space and non-rule lines, and the line-after-write helper (CRLF, no final
newline, several rules, duplicate).
- Relay tests for the new ignore module: discovery, read, append, replace, insert, create, exclude,
and the relative-path rules; an open unmodified buffer reloads after a write.
- Backend contract tests through a fake remote backend whose paths do not exist on this machine:
listing, reading, editing and creating never touch the local filesystem; run the same contract
against `LocalBackend`.
- Pane tests for Undo (Delete, Dirname-removal, Flip, refusal when the file changed), the effect
notice, and the governing-file marker.
- CLAUDE.md: the ignore lines are the named exception to "no hover-only row buttons".
## Decisions
Settled with the user on 2026-11-19 (a question round); folded into the sections above.
- the list: every `.gitignore` of the project, the top one named "project .gitignore"; not
`exclude`, not the global file
- the words: the left pane is the list of `.gitignore` files, the right pane the selected file's
lines; "rail" is not used for them
- two panes side by side; the list takes 35 % of the pane, at least 80 px, the rules the rest
- the area: resizable, width remembered, hidden by default under 600 px (where `p` still opens it);
shared with the preview through a switch
- the line menu: Delete, Dirname, Flip, Open; the hover button is renamed Dirname
- the refusals have their own words: "dirname only works on positive rules", "please edit negation
rules manually", "please edit wildcard rules manually", "no folder above this rule", and "flip
only works on rules"
- the lines have a cursor: `j` / `k` move it, Enter opens at it
- the list does not follow the cursor row; it starts on the project file (else the first file) and
keeps a pick for the session
- every line shown, comments and blank lines too, no numbers; the menu and the hover buttons on
every line
- keys: Purrage's, plus Enter to open in the editor
- after a write: select the file, the new line in the middle of the lines pane, no animation
- ignore I/O goes through `RepoBackend`, with repo-relative paths, so a remote Neovim works
- Purrage is left as it is (frozen); only Ops and the relay backend change
- second round (same day): read only on a `.gitignore` change or an own write, and only the
selected file; hidden panes idle (here only, the app-wide part is its own change); one row height
from the text style (custom font sizes will come); discovery in two steps; the motion keys;
Undo as a button, one at a time; `Delete` deletes a line; the effect of an edit counted; the
marker for files that apply to the row, as a trial; the empty state; `p` under 600 px
- third round: the backend loads the tracked list and selected text in one call, untracked files
later; Undo of a removed line uses a dedicated `insertIgnoreLine`; the governing-file marker is
implemented as a trial in this change; a remote backend must be usable through a fake backend
contract test as well as the manual check
- a `.gitignore` open in Neovim: reload the buffer after a write when it has no unsaved changes;
with unsaved changes, nothing special (the user does not edit them in both at once)
## Ideas for later
- Open in editor, one key everywhere: whatever opens something in the editor (a file row, a
`.gitignore`, a line) uses the same key across the app; Enter here is the first step. Check the
other modes and make them agree.
- A stacked layout as a second choice next to the switch (tiny, low priority): the ignore panes and
the preview both open, the ignore panes above or below the preview, chosen in Settings.
- Dead rules marked: a negation (`!…`) under an excluded folder can never re-include anything. A
separate change: `ops-dead-ignore-rules`.
## Technical notes
- Discovery happens in the backend, as in Purrage: `git ls-files --cached --others
--exclude-standard -- ':(glob)**/.gitignore'` (the root file included); nested untracked files
included, ignored ones skipped.
- `RepoBackend` gains the ignore-file API: `loadIgnorePanes` (tracked list and selected text in one
call), `untrackedIgnoreFiles`, `readIgnoreFile`, `appendIgnoreLines`, `replaceIgnoreLine`,
`insertIgnoreLine`, `createIgnoreFile`, and an `IgnoreFileRef` for a repo-relative `.gitignore`
or the `.git/info/exclude` target. Paths are repo-relative; the backend resolves them and returns
text/lines, never a local absolute path.
- `LocalBackend` delegates to `Repo`; `NvimBackend` calls a new relay module
(`nvimos-relay/lua/nvimos/gitignore.lua`) with its own Lua tests.
- State: `lib/state/ignore_pane.dart` becomes a loaded-once list of files plus the selected one
and the line cursor; tests drive it without widgets.
- The edits reuse `Repo.replaceIgnoreLine`'s semantics (one read, one write, refused when the line
changed), through the backend so it works remotely too; Undo of a removed line uses
`insertIgnoreLine` with the same "line unchanged" check on its neighbours.
- The line-after-write helper is pure and unit-tested: re-read the file, then find the exact rule
line; a duplicate write selects the file without scrolling; several new rules centre the first.
- Open in editor uses `EditorSession.open(relativePath, line)`, not the local editors' root.
- The width and the switch are kept in prefs, like the other remembered sizes; an explicit `p` open
under 600 px is a session override, not a prefs value.
- Purrage reference: `lib/ui/ignore_pane.dart` and `lib/state/ignore_files.dart` in
`~/ws/Purrage`, its `PLAN.md` sections "Where a rule lives" and "The right-hand pane".
- Notes: `nvimos-ops/doc-wip/readme.2026-11-19.ignore-pane.md`.

# an inspect button in the debug build
Tags: ops, debug
Status: Proposed, for TASK-203. Not started.
## Why
Flutter has a select mode that I have seen in the app: click any part of the UI and it outlines that
element and names the widget class behind it. It is the quickest way to learn what a pane, a grid or
a row is called in the code, to name it in a request or find it in `lib/`. Today it only turns on
from outside the app (DevTools, the IDE), and I'm not always sure what turned it on.
## The idea
- In the debug build, a second button next to the debug bar's bug button turns the select mode on
and off.
- While it is on, a click picks the element under the pointer instead of doing what it normally
does: the element is outlined and its class is shown, with its size.
- The release build has no button and no select mode.
## Use cases
- I want to ask for a change to the strip above the diff. I turn inspect on, click the strip, read
`ViewBar`, turn inspect off and write the request with that name.
- I click a row and see `HoverRow`, then the cell inside it and see `PathName`.
## Technical

# rendered markdown in the preview
Tags: ops, ui
Status: Proposed, for TASK-202. Built after `ops-configure` (TASK-204), which makes it a build option.
## Why
The preview pane shows a markdown file as its raw text. A README, a task or a proposal reads better
rendered: headings, lists, tables, code blocks. Sometimes the source is what I want (to check the
markup, to copy a line), so both views are needed.
## The idea
- A markdown file in the preview is shown rendered by default.
- A switch next to the pane's Preview label toggles between Rendered and Text. It is only there for
markdown files and remembers the last choice.
- Rendered markdown stays selectable and copyable, like the text view.
- Code blocks use the same syntax highlighting as the text view; images that point into the repo
resolve against the file's folder.
- Links work like a small browser:
- a local link to another markdown file, followed in the rendered view, opens that file in the
preview
- the mouse's back button goes back to the file I came from, and its forward button goes forward
again, as in a browser; following a new link drops the forward trail
- a web link (`http://`, `https://`) is handed to the system, which opens it the way it opens any
link (the default browser)
- other local links (a file that isn't markdown) open the file the way the preview's Open button
does
- Rendering is a build option: `make configure markdown=off` builds the app without the markdown
package; the preview then shows the text only and has no switch.
## Use cases
- I select `README.md` in Add and Ignore. The preview shows the headings and the table rendered.
- I click `[the plan](PLAN.md)` in it. The preview shows `PLAN.md`; the mouse's back button brings
`README.md` back, the forward button `PLAN.md` again.
- I click `https://docs.flutter.dev/...`. My browser opens the page; the preview stays where it was.
- I want to see why a list breaks. I flip the switch to Text, read the source, flip it back.
- The next markdown file I select opens in the view I left the switch in.
## Technical
- The renderer: `flutter_markdown_plus`, the maintained community fork of `flutter_markdown`, which
flutter.dev discontinued. A `MarkdownBody` widget, built on the pure-Dart `markdown` parser; GFM
tables, task lists, a `syntaxHighlighter` hook for `re_highlight`, `selectable`, an `onTapLink`
callback and an image builder for relative paths.
- others looked at: `markdown_widget` (its own table of contents and theming); the `markdown`
parser with our own widgets (full control, several times the work)
- A build option, like PDF: the package `ops_markdown` in two variants, `packages/ops_markdown_on`
(the renderer) and `packages/ops_markdown_off` (a stub, `markdownBuiltIn = false`); on by default,
since it builds nothing native. `make configure markdown=off` points the dependency at the stub.
- Links
- `onTapLink` gets the href; resolve it against the shown file's folder
- `.md` (and `.markdown`): show that file in the preview, pushing the current one on the history
- `http` / `https` / `mailto`: hand to the system (`ShellExecute` through `cmd /c start ""` or
`explorer.exe`, the same way the Open button launches files; no `url_launcher` needed)
- the app's back stack (`NavHistory`, `lib/ui/nav_history.dart`) only goes back today; it gets a
forward stack: `back()` moves the place it leaves onto forward, `forward()` moves it back, a new
`push` clears forward. The shell maps the mouse's forward button (`kForwardMouseButton`) to it.
That makes forward work for every jump, not only links
- Fit with the project rules
- parse once per file content, not per build (proportional work); a toggle only swaps the shown
child
- the switch is a small atom with tooltips and the pointer cursor; inside the `SelectionArea` its
labels need `SelectionContainer.disabled`; links show the pointer cursor and their target as a
tooltip
- the choice goes into `Prefs`
- check the new package for deprecated APIs and for tooltip semantics (`expectTooltipsInSemantics`)
- Effort: about a day with `flutter_markdown_plus`, plus a few hours for links and the forward
history.

# watch ops' memory over time
Status: Open proposal, not decided, not to be implemented yet. There is no backlog task yet; one gets
made if we go ahead.
## Why
After a while of use, Ops feels slow. A look at the machine on 2026-11-14 found test leftovers (84 git
fsmonitor daemons and 20 orphaned test Neovims, about 880 MB, now cleaned up and stopped at the
source), but that does not settle whether Ops itself leaks. One reading is not enough to tell:
`ops.exe` (the live debug build) was at about 500 MB, and 15 minutes later at about 660 MB, with
hot reloads in between. A debug build under hot reload grows for ordinary reasons (old code and
objects stay around after each reload), so the number alone says little.
## The idea
Measure it over time, in a build where the number means something.
- sample the app's memory (working set) and handle count once a minute while it is in use, and keep
the samples in a small log, so growth over an hour of normal use can be read off as a line
- do it in a profile or release build, not under `make live`, since hot reload skews the numbers
- if the line keeps rising without the work changing (same repo, same mode), it is a leak; if it
rises and levels off, it is the app's normal footprint
Two ways to take the samples, which can also be used together:
- from outside: a small script that reads `ops.exe`'s working set and handle count every minute
(`Get-Process`) into a CSV
- from inside: the app reads its own resident memory (`ProcessInfo.currentRss`) and shows it in the
debug bar, next to the last key and mouse event, plus a line in the log; the debug bar already
exists, so it costs little
- Flutter DevTools' memory tab can show what the Dart heap holds, for the second step: finding what
is growing once it is known that something is
If a leak shows, the first places to look are the ones that keep things alive for the whole session:
the listeners on the session and the state objects, timers (the auto-pick, the Done note, the
retry timer), subscriptions to the backend's git change events, and the per-click records the
timing helper keeps (`UiTiming.instance.samples`).
## Open questions
- profile build or release build for the long run, and how to start it next to the usual
`make live`
- whether the in-app readout is worth keeping, or the outside script is enough
- how long to run it, and what use counts as "normal"
- whether the backend's Neovim (the plugin's watchers and the git event stream) is sampled too
# assign tasks and proposals to milestones by hand
Tags: tasks, milestones
Status: To Do, for TASK-226.
## Why
The Milestones view groups the OpenSpec changes, but where they land is mostly worked out by the
app, not chosen. A change goes to the milestone its task names in the task's `milestone:` field,
else to the dated milestone its archive date falls in, else to "Next". The only way to plan a change
for a milestone is to open its task file and type the field by hand, and a proposal without a task
cannot be planned at all: it sits in "Next" until it is archived.
Planning is the point of milestones. Deciding "this goes into 2027 Q1, that one waits" should be a
click where the item is shown, for a task and for a proposal alike.
## The idea
Every proposal gets exactly one owner of its milestone, so two files can never disagree:
- a proposal linked to a task follows the task: the task's `milestone:` field (Backlog.md's own
field) is the one place it is written
- a proposal without a task carries its own line in `proposal.md`, next to its status:
`Milestone: 2027 Q1`
- a proposal with a task ignores a `Milestone:` line of its own; the detail says where the value
comes from
What the app works out today stays as the fallback: an unplanned archived change goes to the
milestone of its archive date, an unplanned open one to "Next". A milestone chosen by hand always
wins.
The milestones themselves are Backlog.md's own milestone files, not a list Ops invents. Backlog.md
keeps each milestone as a file in `backlog/milestones/` (`m-0 - release-1.0.md`, with an id, a
title, an optional due date and a description) and moves a completed one to
`backlog/archive/milestones/`. Ops reads those, and its "New milestone…" creates one in the same
format, so the Backlog.md CLI and Ops see the same milestones. The deprecated `milestones:` list of
Backlog.md's `config.yml` and a root `milestones.md` are not used. A name that has no file yet
(typed in a task by hand) is still a planned milestone of its own, dated by its name when it reads
as one (`2027 Q1`, `2027-03`, `2027`); without any milestone files the archive months stand in.
A task stores both the name and the id of its milestone: `milestone: Release 1.0` (Backlog.md's key)
and `milestone_id: m-0` next to it. A proposal without a task does the same with `Milestone:` and a
`Milestone-Id:` line right under it; a proposal without a `Status:` line gets the two lines as a
paragraph of their own under its title. The id is what keeps a plan when a milestone is renamed: Ops
reads by the id first when it names a milestone file, else by the name, matched against the ids and
then the titles, ignoring case. When the two disagree the id wins, and the next edit through Ops
writes the current title back: of the task into `milestone:`, of a task-less change (its proposal,
or a box in its `tasks.md`) into `Milestone:`. Just reading never rewrites a file. `milestone_id`
is an Ops key that Backlog.md doesn't know, so its CLI may drop it when it rewrites a task; the name
is then the fallback.
Storing both is a decision, not a workaround to revisit: Backlog.md keeps `milestone:` as a free
string, and its documentation doesn't say whether its CLI writes the id or the title there. Ops
writes the title (readable, and what Backlog.md's own lookup matches) plus the id, and reads either,
so a task written by Backlog.md resolves whichever it holds.
## Use cases
**Planning a task.** Mira opens TASK-140 in the Tasks mode. Under Status and Priority there is now
a Milestone line showing "No milestone". She clicks it, picks "2027 Q1" from the list of
milestones, and the line shows it at once. The task file gets `milestone: 2027 Q1`; its change
moves to 2027 Q1 in the Milestones view.
**Planning a proposal without a task.** Mira opens the change `ops-pdf-pages`, which has no task.
Its properties show the same Milestone menu. She picks "New milestone…", types "v1 launch" and the
due date 2027-05-31. Ops creates `backlog/milestones/m-3 - v1-launch.md`, and the proposal gets
`Milestone: v1 launch` and `Milestone-Id: m-3` under its `Status:` line. "v1 launch" shows up in
the Milestones view with its due date.
**Renaming a milestone.** Mira renames "v1 launch" to "Launch" with the Backlog.md CLI. The tasks
that carry `milestone_id: m-3` stay in it; the next time Ops edits one of them, its `milestone:`
line says "Launch" too.
**Planning a proposal with a task.** On the change `ops-ignore-pane`, linked to TASK-88, the menu
changes TASK-88's `milestone:` field, and the tooltip says so ("from TASK-88"). The proposal file
is not touched.
**Moving things around in the Milestones view.** In the milestone "Next", Mira right-clicks a
change and picks "Move to… 2027 Q2". It moves at once; the change and its task are written the same
way as from the detail panels. "No milestone" takes the plan off again, and the change falls back
to its archive date or "Next".
## Technical
- model: `Change.milestone`, the value of the first `Milestone:` line of `proposal.md`
(`Change.milestoneLine` its index), parsed once like the other change fields
- placement (`Workspace._planMilestones`): `planned(c)` is the task's `milestone` when the change
has a task, else `c.milestone`; `planMilestones` itself does not change
- edits (`lib/tasks/edits.dart`): `taskMilestoneEdit` (like `taskPriorityEdit`: the field replaced,
added before the closing `---`, removed for '') and `changeMilestoneEdit` (the line replaced,
inserted after `Status:` or else after the title, removed for '')
- `Workspace.setTaskMilestone(t, name)` and `setChangeMilestone(c, name)`, the second going to the
task when there is one; optimistic through `edit()`, a `UiTiming` span `tasks.setMilestone`
- UI: a `MilestoneMenu` (a `PopupMenuButton`: "No milestone", the milestones by date, "New
milestone…" with a name field) in the task's and the change's properties; the rows of a
milestone's changes get a right-click menu (`showMenu`) with "Move to…" entries
- every new clickable has the pointer cursor and a tooltip
- milestone files (`lib/tasks/parse.dart`): `parseMilestoneFile` reads `id`, `title`, `due_date`
and `## Description`; `milestoneFilename` (the title lowercased, whitespace to hyphens,
`<>:"/\|?*` removed, at most 50 characters), `nextMilestoneId` (one above the highest in both
folders, `m-0` first) and `newMilestoneFile` follow Backlog.md's `src/file-system/operations.ts`
- `Workspace.createMilestone(title, due:)` writes the file through the backend's `create`, in memory
first; `milestoneFile(id, name)` resolves by id, then name; the edits are `taskMilestoneEdits` /
`changeMilestoneEdits` (the name and the id lines), and `edit()` adds the title fix for a task
whose id names a renamed milestone

# ops PDF preview
Status: To Do (backlog TASK-194)
## Why
Add and Ignore's preview can draw PDF pages through `pdfrx` (PDFium), ported from Purrage. The
library builds PDFium natively, which made every build slow, so it became an optional build
(`packages/ops_pdf_on` / `ops_pdf_off`, `make configure pdf=on|off`). Nothing tests the PDF build: on
2026-11-19 a release went out with PDF on that nobody had tried, and it was set back to a
prerelease. Until this change is done, PDF stays off everywhere: locally, in `make release`, and
in CI.
## What Changes
- a test that builds with PDF on and renders a page of a small sample PDF in the preview (the page
is drawn, its size is right, no error pane)
- a CI job in `test.yml` that runs `tool/configure.ps1 -Pdf on`, then that test, on Windows; it fails the
workflow when the PDF build breaks
- once that job is green: the CI release build (`release.yml`) always builds with PDF on
- local builds stay off: `make release` turns PDF off before it builds (done 2026-11-19);
`make configure pdf=on` stays for trying PDF by hand
- the stub (`ops_pdf_off`) stays as the fallback for builds without PDF
## Scale
PDF is a small feature, one preview adapter among several. Its test is one test among the many CI
already runs, not a gate of its own: it goes into the normal test run (in its own job only because
it needs the PDF build), and a release waits on it the same way it waits on every other test.
- the CI test is the check; no manual checklist is required before PDF ships
- PDF is off in every build until this change is implemented, then always on in CI releases
- the promote flow is a separate change: `ops-release-promote`
## Impact
- `nvimos-poc-frontend/test/`: a PDF preview test and a sample PDF fixture (small, checked in)
- `nvimos-poc-frontend/.github/workflows/test.yml`: a PDF job
- `nvimos-poc-frontend/.github/workflows/release.yml`: pdf-on before the build
- open: the test must skip in the default (off) build, where `ops_pdf` is the stub; a tag or a
separate test file run only by the PDF job
- open: CI time for the PDFium build, and whether `flutter-action`'s cache keeps it
## ADDED Requirements
### Requirement: PDF build is tested before it ships
The PDF preview (pdfrx) SHALL ship in a release only from a build whose PDF test passed in CI.
Until that test exists, every build SHALL be made with PDF off.
#### Scenario: Release before the test exists
- **WHEN** `make release` or the CI release runs before this change is implemented
- **THEN** the build has PDF off, and a PDF in the preview shows its facts and the Open button
#### Scenario: CI test
- **WHEN** CI runs the PDF job
- **THEN** it builds with PDF on and renders the first page of a sample PDF in the preview, and a
failure fails the workflow
#### Scenario: Release after the test exists
- **WHEN** the CI release builds after the PDF job is in place
- **THEN** it builds with PDF on
### Requirement: Local builds stay quick
Local builds SHALL have PDF off unless the developer turns it on with `make configure pdf=on`.
#### Scenario: Local release
- **WHEN** `make release` runs locally
- **THEN** it turns PDF off before it builds, and PDF is still off afterwards
