# provision the relay plugin on first run
Status: Open proposal, not decided, not to be implemented yet. There is no backlog task yet; one gets
made if we go ahead.
## Why
Ops offers to start Neovim from the Connect screen, but the offer only works when relay can be found.
Today `findBackendDir` checks `NVIMOS_BACKEND`, then a `relay` or `nvimos-poc-backend` checkout next
to the app, and otherwise starts Neovim with `-c NvimosServe` and trusts the user's own config to
provide relay. A default Neovim install has no relay, and plain `nvim` does not put it on
`runtimepath`. So on a machine without the author's setup, ops starts Neovim and then cannot attach:
the first experience is a Connect screen that promises something it cannot deliver.
There is a second inconsistency behind the same gap. The Connect screen resolves the plugin from the
filesystem, while Directories' New Neovim per directory asks an already-connected Neovim for
`plugin_root()` and then calls a separate launcher in `dirs.dart`. That path cannot bootstrap; it only
works because another Neovim is already running with the plugin.
## The idea
Give ops its own copy of relay, and make every start go through one resolver and one launcher.
The round on 2026-11-18 settled these choices:
- when no local plugin can be found, download relay into `%APPDATA%/nvimos/plugin` and start Neovim
with that copy
- search order: `NVIMOS_BACKEND`, then a local checkout, then the managed download; the user's own
config is the last fallback, not the first
- download the archive of `nvimos/relay` `main`, newest first
- refresh the managed copy when it is older than six hours; if the refresh fails, keep the existing
copy
- if no managed copy exists and the download fails, fall back to `:NvimosServe` in the user's config
- ship a known relay plugin inside the installer, so an offline first run has something to seed the
managed folder with, and refresh it from downloads afterwards
- when `nvim` is not on PATH either, offer to download a portable Neovim into the app state folder
- unify the Connect-screen launcher and the Directories launcher into one implementation
The state folder would hold the managed plugin, the portable Neovim and the fetch metadata:
%APPDATA%/nvimos/
state.json
plugin/       relay checkout: plugin/nvimos.lua, lua/nvimos/...
nvim/         portable Neovim (bin/nvim.exe, runtime/...)
plugin.json   fetchedAt, source, revision, API version
The resolution order becomes:
NVIMOS_BACKEND
> local checkout (relay or nvimos-poc-backend next to the app)
> %APPDATA%/nvimos/plugin (managed download)
> NvimosServe in the user's config
> error with setup steps
The bundled plugin seeds the managed folder on first start if it is missing, so first run needs no
network. A stale managed copy is refreshed atomically: fetch into a sibling temp folder, check for
`plugin/nvimos.lua`, rename into place, and keep the old copy on any failure.
One function then owns the whole start: resolve the plugin, choose the executable (system Neovim or
the portable one), build the command line for console, nvim-qt or headless, set the working
directory, launch, and poll the address. The Connect screen calls it with an address; Directories
calls it with a directory and a fresh port. `DirsState.launch` can stay as the test seam but should
delegate to the same implementation.
First run, in order: no `nvim` gets the portable download offer; no plugin gets the bundled seed or
the download; Neovim starts with the resolved plugin on `runtimepath`; the app connects and shows the
opening mode; the managed copy is refreshed in the background when it turns six hours old.
## A simpler shape (added later, not decided)
Most of the complexity above comes from treating the plugin as something the app acquires at runtime.
Relay is about 126 KB of Lua across 33 files, and its API is coupled to the app (`Backend.apiVersion`
is `1`). It is not a large third-party dependency; it is part of the product, so its lifecycle could
match the app's lifecycle.
That would replace the download, refresh, bundle/seed and API-skew decisions with:
- embed relay in ops as Flutter assets; copy them to a state folder on startup, overwriting every
time (126 KB is nothing), with no `plugin.json`, timestamps or version folders
- resolve the plugin in two cases only: `NVIMOS_BACKEND` when set (the developer override), otherwise
the embedded copy
- drop the GitHub download and the archive of `main`, the six-hour refresh, the bundle-vs-download
split and the seeding step, the checksums and atomic replace, the stale-copy handling, the
`NvimosServe` fallback, and the sibling checkout search
- drop the portable Neovim download for now: show that Neovim is missing, link to an install, and
retry. The people this app is for already run Neovim; bundling or downloading an editor is a
bigger decision and a larger maintenance surface, and can be revisited if first-run feedback says
missing `nvim` is common
- keep the one-launcher refactor: it is independent of provisioning and small
The trade-off is that plugin fixes ship with an ops release instead of instantly. Given the API
handshake, that is arguably correct: a newer `main` plugin can break an older app, which is the risk
the download design spends the most words on. The installer would grow by about 126 KB.
The state-folder path and the resolution order in the two ideas above are not settled; the simpler
shape would make most of those paths unnecessary. In short: embedded plugin, system Neovim, one
launcher, no downloader.

copy will be used and whether a refresh is in flight?

# the rail in the user's order
Tags: ops, ui
Status: In progress, for TASK-200.
## Why
The mode rail listed the modes in a fixed order, and every mode was always there. Someone who lives
in Changes and Tasks and never opens History wants those two on top and History gone, without
losing the way back to it.
## The idea
- Drag an icon up or down the rail to move its mode. A drop line shows where it will land, on the
side the mode ends up. The order is saved in the state file and the next start uses it.
- Right-click an icon to hide its mode. Alt+1..9, Alt+[ / Alt+] and the wheel skip hidden modes.
At least one mode stays. Settings lists the hidden ones and shows one again in the place it was
dragged to; **Reset the rail** restores the default order and shows every mode.
- The saved order and hidden set are mode names: a name that no longer exists is dropped, a new
mode comes last, duplicates go.
- A click is not a drag. A press picks the icon up only after the pointer has travelled far enough,
so the small movement that comes with a click still opens the mode.
## Use cases
- I click Changes and my hand moves a few pixels as I press. Changes opens; the icon doesn't dim
and nothing follows the pointer.
- I press Tasks and pull it up the rail. After a short distance the icon lifts, the drop line shows
under Pull request, and on release Tasks is second.
- On the touchscreen I tap a mode with a finger. The tap opens it; a finger needs to travel further
than a mouse before a drag starts.
## Technical
- Shipped (ops commits `3553ec5`, `7027b7a`): `RailState` in `lib/ui/mode_rail.dart`, the rail's
`Draggable` / `DragTarget` rows, the Settings list and reset.
- Drag threshold: Flutter's `Draggable` uses `ImmediateMultiDragGestureRecognizer`, whose slop for a
mouse is `kPrecisePointerHitSlop`, 1 px. Any wobble during a click started a drag and the click
was lost. Windows' own threshold is about 4 px (`SM_CXDRAG`), macOS and browser drag-and-drop
3-5 px. The rail uses 8 px for a mouse.
- `ThresholdDraggable` (`lib/ui/threshold_draggable.dart`) overrides `Draggable.createRecognizer`
with a `ThresholdMultiDragGestureRecognizer`: it claims the pointer once it has moved more than
`max(kDragThreshold, computeHitSlop(kind))`, so a mouse needs 8 px and a finger Flutter's touch
slop (`kTouchSlop`, 18 px)
- mouse and touch are told apart by the pointer kind: the Windows embedder reports a finger as
`PointerDeviceKind.touch` and a mouse as `mouse` (pen as `stylus`); nothing app-side is needed
- the drag starts at the press point and the travel is applied at once, so the feedback appears
under the pointer (`pointerDragAnchorStrategy`)
# Tasks

## 2. Drag threshold
- [x] 2.1 `ThresholdDraggable`: a press becomes a drag only after 8 px for a mouse, Flutter's touch
slop (18 px) for a finger; below that it stays a click
- [x] 2.2 widget test: a 5 px wobble opens the mode, a 12 px move picks the icon up
- [ ] 2.3 try it in the app with the mouse: a click never lifts the icon, a drag doesn't feel sticky
- [ ] 2.4 verify on the touchscreen: a tap opens the mode, a drag with a finger reorders, and the
rail doesn't scroll instead (does the Windows embedder deliver touch as `PointerDeviceKind.touch`
there, and is 18 px right for a finger?)
# ops release promote
Status: To Do (backlog TASK-195)
## Why
The weekly CI release (`release.yml`, Wednesdays) builds and publishes straight to a release, and
GitHub marks it Latest. Nobody has tried that build first. On 2026-11-19 an untested build became
Latest and had to be set back to a prerelease by hand. A build should be tested before it becomes
the release people download.
## What Changes
- the scheduled release publishes a **prerelease** (`vYYYY-MM-DD`, not Latest), as today's gate and
build already do, only the flag changes
- a new manual workflow, **promote** (`workflow_dispatch`, input: the tag, default the newest
prerelease): it turns that prerelease into the release and marks it Latest
- promote only takes a prerelease that exists; it builds nothing, so the promoted files are exactly
the ones that were tested
- `make release` (local) publishes a prerelease too, so a local upload also waits for promote
- a local `make promote TAG=` runs the same `gh release edit` for when CI is not at hand
- flow: build, then promote (not artifact-only, not the automatic weekly Latest)
- separate from the PDF change (`ops-pdf-preview`)
## Impact
- `nvimos-poc-frontend/.github/workflows/release.yml`: `gh release create --prerelease`
- new `nvimos-poc-frontend/.github/workflows/promote.yml`
- `nvimos-poc-frontend/Makefile`: `release` adds `--prerelease`; a new `promote` target
- the weekly gate counts prereleases as releases, so an unpromoted build doesn't start a new one
every week (open: or it should, and older prereleases get pruned)
## ADDED Requirements
### Requirement: Builds publish as prereleases
A release build, from CI or from `make release`, SHALL publish as a prerelease, never as Latest.
#### Scenario: Weekly build
- **WHEN** the scheduled release workflow builds and publishes
- **THEN** the new GitHub release is a prerelease, and the previous Latest stays Latest
### Requirement: Promote a tested build
A manual promote step SHALL turn a chosen prerelease into the Latest release without building
again.
#### Scenario: Promote
- **WHEN** promote runs with a prerelease's tag
- **THEN** that release is no longer a prerelease and is marked Latest, with the same files
#### Scenario: Wrong tag
- **WHEN** promote runs with a tag that is not a prerelease
- **THEN** it fails and changes nothing
# Tasks

## 2. Promote

## 3. Verify

# Untrusted repositories: the security posture
Tags: security, ops
Status: Proposed, for TASK-205. The P0 fixes below are in scope; the remaining findings are
follow-ups named at the end.
## Why
Ops is a local app, so it is tempting to assume it runs on local trust. That assumption is wrong in
one specific way: the app's input is a repository, and a repository is not just data. It is a tree of
files chosen by someone else, a `.git` directory that can carry configuration and hooks, prose the
app renders, and prose an agent reads.
Local trust holds for the files the user wrote. It does not hold for a branch from a fork reviewed as
a pull request, a take-home exercise, a sample repo downloaded as a zip, a repo an agent created or
edited, or a Neovim the user connected to over the network. "The app runs locally" says where the
process runs, not who controls its input.
The risks are not exotic. Each one is a normal feature doing what it was told:
- Mara reviews a contributor's branch. The README has `[Check the build](ms-msdt:...)`. She clicks it.
- She opens a sample project from a zip. Its `.git/config` sets `core.fsmonitor`, or its
`.git/hooks/pre-commit` exists. She stages a file and commits a typo fix.
- She presses **New change** in a repo whose `openspec/config.yaml` says, in prose, to append a line
to `.git/hooks/post-checkout` first. The agent is told to follow that file, and may write.
- She runs `:NvimosServe 0.0.0.0:6666` to reach the app from a laptop, and the cafe Wi-Fi gets the
same power her shell has.
- The repo folder is named `acme & calc`, and the app starts Neovim through `cmd /c start`.
## The model
Three rules, in order:
1. **Repository content is data, never instructions.** It may be rendered, diffed and read. It does
not get to direct a tool with more power than the pane that shows it.
2. **Opening, browsing and reviewing must not execute code from the repo.** Staging, committing,
merging and checking out may run the user's own tooling, and only after the app says so.
3. **Everything that leaves the process goes through one named door with a test:** a shell, a URL, a
socket, an agent. No second path, no `cmd /c` shortcut.
## Findings
In scope here: S1–S6, S8 and S12. S7 and S9–S11 are the named follow-ups at the end.
| # | Risk | Where | How it happens | Severity |

| S1 | An auto-approving agent follows repo prose | `lib/tasks/workspace.dart` (`newChange`) | `claude -p --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep`; the prompt says to follow `openspec/config.yaml` and the existing changes | High |

| S2 | The relay is unauthenticated remote code execution | `nvimos-relay` (`serve`), `lib/rpc/client.dart` | any client that reaches the port can call `nvim_exec_lua` and `nvimos.files.*` (absolute paths); `serve` accepts `0.0.0.0`; the app connects to any host in cleartext | High |

| S3 | Git runs repository config and hooks | `lib/local/repo.dart`, `local_backend.dart` | `status` runs `core.fsmonitor`; `diff` runs textconv drivers; `commit`, `checkout`, `merge` and `rebase` run hooks and filters | Medium |

| S4 | Rendered markdown hands URLs and files to the Windows shell | `lib/state/preview_links.dart`, `local/file_manager.dart` | any non-`file` scheme becomes a `WebLink`; any local path becomes a `FileLink`; both end at `explorer.exe` | High |
| S5 | `cmd /c start` re-parses arguments | `nvim_launcher.dart`, `repos.dart`, `editors.dart`, `terminals.dart` | a directory or file name with `&`, `\|`, `^`, `%` can start another command | High |

| S6 | Paths are joined, not contained | `local/paths.dart`, `files.dart`, `local_backend.dart`, relay `tracking.lua` | `.nvimos`, `readFiles`, ignore writes and the relay's `repo.path()` accept absolute paths and `..`; discard deletes untracked paths for good | Medium |
| S7 | Native parsers read repo files in-process | `packages/ops_pdf_on` (PDFium), image previews | a malformed PDF or image can exercise a memory-safety bug | Low |

| S8 | Logs and traces keep more than they should | `log_state.dart`, `action_failure.dart`, `_git`'s `detail` | command lines, home paths, credentials in remote URLs, and whatever a failure quotes (a path, a diff line) are copyable | Medium |
| S9 | Releases are unsigned and packed | `.github/workflows/release.yml`, `dist/` | no Authenticode, no checksum, Enigma Virtual Box packing; AV heuristics and SmartScreen | Medium |
| S10 | CI actions float on tags | `.github/workflows/*.yml` | `actions/checkout@v4` and friends can move under the build | Low |
| S11 | The RPC decoder has no frame cap | `lib/rpc/msgpack.dart` | a peer can make the app allocate without bound | Low |

| S12 | Backend discovery can load a repo's Neovim plugin | `lib/state/nvim_launcher.dart` (`findBackendDir`) | it walks up from `Directory.current`, so a repo containing `relay/plugin/nvimos.lua` is added to Neovim's runtimepath and `:runtime` executes it | Medium |
What is already right, and should stay:
- every process starts with `runInShell: false`, and git gets `--` before paths;
- `diff` and `diffFile` already pass `--no-ext-diff`;
- deletes in Add and Ignore go to the Recycle Bin by default, and `HiddenWrite` restores attributes;
- the hot-reload VM-service path is guarded by `kDebugMode`;
- `pubspec.lock` is committed;
- git's own `safe.directory` refusal is not bypassed.
## What this change fixes
### S1. The agent drafts; the app writes
- Default to a read-only draft. The agent runs with no `Write`/`Edit` tools (or `--permission-mode
plan`) and returns the proposed files; the app validates and writes only
`openspec/changes/<id>/…` and the matching `backlog/tasks/task-<n> - <slug>.md`.
- Never write `.git/**`. Refuse a `tracking` root outside the repo unless the user confirms it for
this change.
- Show the prompt and the resulting diff before anything is written. `acceptEdits` is not a default;
it is an explicit second confirmation, and still limited to the change directory.
- Treat quoted repository prose as data in the prompt. The sandbox, not the wording, is the defense.
### S2. The relay is loopback, and remote is said out loud
- `:NvimosServe` refuses a non-loopback address unless called with `!`; the notice says the port is
open to the network and unencrypted. Loopback is not a per-user boundary on Windows either: another
account on the machine can connect to `127.0.0.1`, which is why the named pipe is the real local fix.
- The app defaults to `127.0.0.1`, marks a non-loopback connection `remote, unencrypted`, explains
that anyone on the path can read and change the session, and does not remember it.
- Document the supported remote path: SSH port forwarding, or a Neovim on the same machine.
- Do not pretend a token fixes this. A token on `nvimos.attach` cannot protect `nvim_exec_lua`:
Neovim answers every client on that address with its full API. Only binding and transport do.
### S3. Git is told to ignore repository tooling
A clean `git clone` does not copy hooks or `.git/config`, so this is not "every clone is remote code
execution". It is every repository that arrives with its `.git` directory: a zip, a shared folder, a
VM snapshot, a repo an agent created. The app's own agent can write `.git` today, which is how S1
turns into S3.
- One wrapper for every git call (replace `GitDir.runCommand` where it is used) that adds:
`-c core.fsmonitor=false -c core.pager=cat -c core.editor=false -c sequence.editor=false`,
`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, and `--no-textconv` on patch-producing calls (`--no-ext-diff` stays).
- For write operations (`add`, `commit`, `checkout`, `merge`, `rebase`), preflight with
`git config --local --list`: when the repo defines `filter.*.clean|smudge|process`,
`core.fsmonitor`, `core.hooksPath`, `core.sshCommand`, or `credential.helper`, refuse with one
notice that names the key and says to commit in a terminal if the user trusts it.
- Never run hooks from the app: point `core.hooksPath` at an empty temp directory (that disables all
hooks, including `post-checkout`), and still pass `--no-verify` to commit. A repo that has hooks
gets the notice instead.
- Make the notice name the file and key, not a generic "unsafe repository".
### S4. Links are classified, not forwarded
- A pure `classifyLink(href)` returns `openWeb(url)` only for `http`, `https` and `mailto`.
- Every other scheme (`ms-msdt:`, `search-ms:`, `smb:`, `javascript:`, `data:`, unknown) is shown as
text with a **Copy** button. It never reaches ShellExecute.
- `file:` and local paths resolve inside the preview. Opening one is a second, explicit click that
names the resolved absolute path; a UNC path (`\\server\share`, `file://server/share`) is refused,
because passing it to Explorer leaks an NTLM hash.
- `Run` on an executable stays the only path to executing a repo file, and the button shows the
absolute target.
### S5. No `cmd /c start`
- Replace the four call sites with `ShellExecuteW` through FFI (as `shell_delete.dart` already does),
or with a direct `Process.start` plus `CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE` for console programs. On macOS and Linux
the same `ShellLauncher` wraps `open` and `xdg-open`; the allowlist and the no-shell rule are
identical, and the UNC refusal is Windows-only.
- A `.cmd`/`.bat` shim is opened with ShellExecute, which handles the association without a shell.
- If any `cmd` use survives, quote and reject `& | ^ < > ( ) % ! "` in the argument it carries. A
test uses a folder named `a & b` and asserts that only Neovim starts.
### S6. Writes and deletes are contained
- Add `resolveInside(root, path)`: canonicalize, resolve links, compare case-insensitively with the
root prefix, and reject `..` and absolute paths that leave it. Use it for task files, ignore files,
discard, rename and the relay's `repo.path()`.
- `.nvimos tracking` may point outside the repo (it is the point of the file), but the app asks once
per repo before writing there, and says the resolved path.
- `discard()` on an untracked row goes to the trash when `deleteToTrash` is on, like Add and Ignore.
- Never recurse through a link: check `FileSystemEntity.isLink` before a recursive delete, and name
the resolved target in the confirmation.
### S8. Traces are redacted
- Before an error or a log row is stored, replace the home directory with `~`, strip `user:pass@`
from URLs, and cap the detail. The copy button copies the same redacted text.
### S12. Only the app's own relay may be loaded
- `findBackendDir` searches `NVIMOS_BACKEND`, the exe's folder and `~/ws`, never the folder being
opened. The resolved plugin path is printed in the Log, and a path inside the opened repo is
refused with a notice.
- The search stops at the first match; it does not walk to the drive root through a checkout.
## Out of scope, named
- `ops-release-integrity`: Authenticode signing or a published `SHA256SUMS`, a version display, and
pinned action SHAs. The Enigma Virtual Box single-file build should at least say what it is.
- `ops-preview-sandbox`: PDF and image parsing out of process, or PDF off by default in releases.
- `relay-local-socket`: a Windows named pipe or Unix socket for the relay, so the OS can scope access
to the user. This is the real fix for S2's local-process case; it needs a Neovim-side design.
- RPC frame caps (S11) go with the relay work.
## Decisions
Settled defaults; the alternative is named where it matters.
- **Untrusted by default.** No trust prompt on open. The app is safe to browse first; the notice
appears only when a repo actually carries the thing being refused.
- **The app never runs repo hooks.** Not behind a flag, not after a trust dialog. If the user wants
hooks, they commit in Neovim or a terminal. A "trust this repo" switch is not worth the risk it
implies.
- **The agent never holds the pen by default.** It drafts, the app writes the two places a change
owns. This removes S1 rather than moderating it.
- **Links: http, https, mailto only.** `file:` links stay inside the preview. Unknown schemes are
text plus Copy.
- **Remote relay is a session choice, never a stored default.** Saying it is unencrypted is part of
the connect flow, not a tooltip.
- **Discard is reversible when the setting says so.** The trash setting applies to every delete,
including discard.
- **No security theatre.** No token that does not cover `nvim_exec_lua`; no warning that fires on
every open.
## Usability
- Browsing a normal, clean repository changes nothing on screen. The notices are for repos that carry
hooks, exec-capable config, a tracking root outside the checkout, or a repo-born link.
- A refusal is one sentence plus the key or path that caused it, with Details in the Log, in the
same voice as the rest of the app.
- `Help` gains a `Security` group: what the app runs, what it refuses, and the remote caveat.
- The connect screen shows `local` or `remote, unencrypted` next to the address, and the status bar
keeps the badge for the session.
## Technical notes
- Link classification is pure and lives beside `preview_links.dart`: `classifyLink(href)`, with tests
for every scheme above, control characters, `\\server\share`, `C:\…`, `..\..\…`, and a fragment.
- Shell launching goes through one `ShellLauncher` seam with a fake, like `ProcessRunner`; the Windows
call is `ShellExecuteW(NULL, "open", path, NULL, cwd, SW_SHOWNORMAL)`, with `open` / `xdg-open` on
macOS and Linux behind the same interface. The fixes here must not add new Windows-only code to the
paths that already have platform branches (`editors.dart`, `terminals.dart`, `trash.dart`).
- Git hardening lives in one place: `Repo`'s runner and `LocalBackend._git` share a `GitCommand`
builder, so no call site can forget the flags. The preflight parses
`git config --local --list -z` into a set of keys and refuses by key.
- `resolveInside` uses `FileSystemEntity.resolveSymbolicLinks` where the path exists, and the
canonical root otherwise; both sides are lowercased on Windows only.
- The relay's `serve(addr)` gains a loopback check (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`); `serve!` or a
second confirmation is the only way past it. `test_05_nav.lua` covers both.
- The hostile fixture is a checked-in directory that the test copies to a temp dir: a `.git/config`
with `core.fsmonitor` and `filter.x.process`, a hook that writes a marker, a README with the six
link shapes, a junction to an outside dir, a file named `a & b`, and a `.nvimos` pointing at a temp
sibling.
- `SECURITY.md` states the threat model in one page: what is trusted (the user, the machine, the
editor), what is not (the repo, its config, its prose, the network), and what the app does about
each.
## Done means
1. The hostile fixture is opened, browsed, diffed and committed in a test. No marker file appears, no
command from its config or hooks runs, and one notice names each refusal.
2. The six link shapes are classified by unit test; `ms-msdt:`, `search-ms:`, `smb:`,
`javascript:`, `data:` and `file://server/share` reach no shell; `http`/`https`/`mailto` do.
3. A repo folder named `a & b` opens Neovim and starts nothing else.
4. `:NvimosServe 0.0.0.0:6666` refuses without `!`; the app refuses a non-loopback address without
the explicit remote confirmation, and does not persist it.
5. **New change** on a repo whose prose asks for `.git/hooks/post-checkout` writes only inside the
change directory and the task file.
6. Discard on an untracked row lands in the trash when the setting is on.
7. Starting Neovim from inside a repo with a fake `relay/plugin/nvimos.lua` does not load it, and the
Log names the plugin that was loaded.
8. `make test` and `flutter analyze` pass; `SECURITY.md` and the Help group exist.
## Ideas for later
- A per-repo "trusted" flag that unlocks hooks and agent writes, if the refusals prove too blunt.
- Open-with on a file link could go through the preview's own viewer first, for every type.
- A signed update check, once there is a certificate decision.

# snappy UI checks: responsiveness as a test that fails
Tags: performance, tests
Status: To Do, for TASK-225.
## Why
Moving through the Tasks list was slow enough to feel broken. On a project with 62 open tasks, every
Up / Down or click on a task took a visible moment before the highlight and the detail followed.
The app's own timing log agreed: `input.click→frame` had a p95 of 615 ms.
Finding out why took a debugging session (2026-11-28): a throwaway widget test on a copy of
`nvimos-meta` (192 tasks), a CPU profile through the VM service, and counting what rebuilt. It
found two things:
- **Per-read parsing.** `Task.labels`, the checklists, and `Change.taskId` / `status` / `stage`
were getters that parsed the front matter or the proposal again on every read; `taskId` built a
`RegExp` per call. The sidebar's Inbox count walks every task, change and branch through them:
15 ms per build, the label counts another 4.5 ms. The sidebar is built on every cursor move.
Fixed in that session (parsed once, counts cached until the data changes).
- **The whole view rebuilds on a selection.** A cursor move rebuilds the entire Tasks view, about
4,400 elements, the sidebar included, and builds the new task's detail panel from scratch. After
the first fix a `j` press still took about 150 ms p50 in the widget test (up to 380 ms). Not
fixed yet.
Both are the kind of bug CLAUDE.md already warns about (proportional work), and both came back
after earlier passes on other modes. A rule in a document does not stop the next getter from
parsing per read. A test that fails does.
## The idea
Responsiveness becomes a maintained check, run while developing, not a session of debugging when
it already hurts. A fixed, realistic data set is the input; a set of tests drives the interactions
a user does all day and fails when one costs more than its budget.
### The fixture
A snapshot of a real project's planning data: today's `nvimos-meta` with its 192 tasks, its
OpenSpec changes, the milestones and the branches. It is checked in as one blob and unpacked into a
temp repo for the test (through `keepForCleanup`, like every test repo).
Two ways to store it:
- **The files** (a zip of `backlog/`, `openspec/`, `milestones.md`, `index.tsv`, plus a list of
branch names with dates). The test reads them through the real load path, so the parse cost is in
the measurement too, and the fixture can be refreshed from the project with one command.
- **The parsed workspace as JSON.** Faster to set up and needs no Neovim, but it skips the parser
and goes stale the moment the model changes shape.
The files are the better choice: they keep the parse path in the measurement, and they survive
model changes. The fixture is refreshed on purpose (a `make` target), not on every run, so the
numbers stay comparable.
### What is checked
The Tasks mode first. Each of these views:
- Inbox
- Open tasks
- To Do, In Progress, Needs Test, Done, Dropped
- All tasks
- Changes
- Milestones
Legacy notes are left out: they won't be in the final app.
In each view, these interactions, measured from the input to the painted frame:
- cursor move (`j` / `k`), a few in a row
- a click on a row
- opening the detail (Right into the panel)
- switching to the view from the sidebar
Other modes follow once the Tasks checks are in place; the harness is the same.
## How to run it: three options
### a. Timing in a widget test
What the debugging session did (`test/tasks_move_timing_test.dart` in the frontend): pump the view
on the test clock, send the key, `pump()`, and time it with a `Stopwatch`.
- runs in `make test`, a few seconds
- measures debug JIT cost, several times what the release app costs, and noisy: the same move
varied from 120 to 380 ms
- a threshold must be loose to not flake, so it catches a 10x regression, not a 2x one
### b. Structural budgets
Count work instead of time, so the result does not depend on the machine:
- widgets rebuilt per interaction (`debugOnRebuildDirtyWidget`)
- elements mounted per interaction (a new detail panel is expected, a new sidebar is not)
- calls of the expensive functions: `inbox()`, the parsers, `rows()` rebuilding
- derived data kept: after a cursor move `rows()` and the sidebar counts are `identical` to before
Deterministic, so it can gate `make test` without flaking. It doesn't say how long something
takes; it says the cascade stayed small, which is what goes wrong.
### c. Frame timings in the real app
A profile-mode `integration_test` on the Windows app: start it on the fixture, drive the same
interactions, read `FrameTiming` (build and raster per frame) or `traceAction`.
- closest to what the user feels
- slower (a profile build) and machine-dependent: a separate target, `make snappy`, not
`make test`
### Recommendation
A mix:
- **b** as the gate in `make test`: it fails on the bugs we have actually had (a cascade, a
per-read parse), on any machine
- **a** with generous thresholds and a printed table per view and interaction, so a run shows where
the time goes and a big regression still fails
- **c** now and then, before a release, as `make snappy`; its numbers are the ones the thresholds
are eventually set from
## Thresholds
Open; these are starting numbers, tightened as the code gets faster:
- profile mode (c): a cursor move fits one frame, **16 ms**; a click or a view switch **50 ms**
- widget test (a): a cursor move under **100 ms** p50 on the fixture to start (it is about 150 ms
today), lowered as the rebuild is narrowed
- structural (b): a cursor move rebuilds no sidebar entry, recomputes no row list and no count,
and mounts nothing outside the list rows and the detail panel
## Technical notes
- Reuse the debugging test's pieces: `bigPlanRepo` / a fixture unpacker, `TestNvim`, the
`debugOnRebuildDirtyWidget` counter, and the VM-service CPU profile (behind a flag, for
diagnosing a failure, not for the gate; it needs `--enable-vmservice` and `vm_service` as a
dev dependency).
- Tests that point the app at a repo set `APPDATA` to a temp folder, or `Prefs` and `UiTiming`
write into the user's `%APPDATA%/nvimos`.
- `UiTiming` spans `tasks.move` and `tasks.select` with `markPainted()`, as the shell and Add and
Ignore have, so `make timings` shows the same interactions from the real app.
- Follow-up found by the session: a selection-only notice should rebuild only the list rows and
the detail panel, not the sidebar or the header (a separate listenable for the selection, or the
sidebar behind its own `ListenableBuilder` on data notices only). The structural budget for a
cursor move pins it.
- The fixture refresh copies the planning files and the branch list from a project; it never
writes there.
# Tasks
## 1. Build
- [x] 1.1 the fixture: a gzipped JSON (not a zip: Dart reads gzip without a package) of
`nvimos-meta`'s planning files with their mtimes and its branches (commits ahead, dates), in the
frontend's `test/fixtures/tasks_snappy.json.gz`; `make snapshot from=<repo>` refreshes it; tests
unpack it into a temp repo (one `git fast-import`) through `keepForCleanup`
- [x] 1.2 a harness that opens the Tasks mode on the fixture in a widget test, with `Prefs` in a

- [x] 1.3 structural budgets per view and interaction: widgets built per interaction, a move or a

- [x] 1.4 timings per view and interaction (switch, open, cursor move, row click, opening the

Changes, Milestones (not Legacy notes)
- [x] 1.6 `UiTiming` spans `tasks.move` and `tasks.select` with `markPainted()`
- [ ] 1.7 a profile-mode `integration_test` on the Windows app with frame timings for the same

- [x] 1.8 a selection-only notice rebuilds only the list rows and the detail panel; the

## 2. Verify

# tooltips without orphan accessibility nodes
Tags: accessibility, ui
Status: In progress, for TASK-199.
## Why
`make live` fills the log with bursts of the same line:
[ERROR:flutter/shell/platform/common/accessibility_bridge.cc(114)] Failed to update ui::AXTree, error: 2495 will not be in the tree and is not the new root
The Windows accessibility bridge (the part of the Flutter engine that hands the semantics tree to
Narrator and other screen readers) refuses an update that contains a node no parent lists. A screen
reader then misses that node, and the log is noisy enough to hide real errors.
The id in the message is the next free one, so it doesn't say which widget it was. One tooltip
shown once is enough to produce a whole burst: its bubble's node is sent again on every frame of
the fade in and out.
This is a different cause from the earlier error 144 (hidden modes in the `IndexedStack`), which
`ExcludeSemantics` on the hidden modes addressed.
## The cause
On desktop a tooltip's bubble is drawn in the root overlay, far from the widget it explains. Flutter
moves the bubble's semantics node under the tooltip's owner, so a screen reader meets it in the right
place: the tooltip's `OverlayPortal` tags its owner with a `traversalParentIdentifier`, and the
bubble carries the matching `traversalChildIdentifier`.
When several such owners merge into one semantics node, Flutter keeps only the first identifier
(`SemanticsConfiguration.absorb` in `semantics.dart`:
`_traversalParentIdentifier ??= child._traversalParentIdentifier`, Flutter 3.50). This happens, for
example, in a tappable row with a tooltip on its state letter and a second tooltip somewhere else.
Showing the second tooltip then makes a bubble that has no traversal parent. Flutter drops it from
its own hit-test and traversal lists but still sends it as a dirty node, and the bridge rejects it.
Reproduced in a widget test: two tooltips inside one tappable node; showing the first leaves no
orphan, showing the second leaves one; the same second tooltip wrapped in
`Semantics(container: true)` leaves none. A single tooltip in a tappable node is fine.
## The idea
- A tooltip that would share a semantics node with another overlay portal (a second tooltip, a menu
anchor, an autocomplete) gets a node of its own: `Semantics(container: true)` around it, or
around the smallest part that holds it.
- A test helper shows every tooltip on a screen, one at a time, and fails when it leaves an
orphan overlay node: one that is attached to the semantics tree but cannot be reached from the
root in traversal order, the order the engine builds the platform tree from. The view tests call
it for their mode, so the next nested tooltip fails a test instead of the log.
- Look for the same kind of problem in other places: anything that sends a semantics node the
platform tree can't hold.
## Where it applies
What the helper and a set of probes found (2026-11-20).
Merged tooltips, the cause above:
- Add and Ignore: the "The highlighted files (v)" tab of the side pane switch (`_SideTab`,
`lib/ui/add_ignore_view.dart`) leaves an orphan; the other tooltips of the view, the rows
included, are fine
- clean with the helper: Repos, the Ignore dialog and the Ignore pane, Settings, Log, the rev picker,
the status bar, the preview pane, the merge actions, the commit message, the Tasks list and detail
panel
- not covered yet, the view tests end on a screen without tooltips: Directories, the network
dialog, the checkout dialog, Help; Pull request and Changes have no widget test of their own with
data
Similar problems, the same orphan by another way:
- **a mode switch while a tooltip is shown.** The bubble is in the root overlay, outside the
mode's `ExcludeSemantics` and outside the `IndexedStack`'s offstage child; when the owner's mode
is hidden, the owner's node goes and the bubble stays. Both probes (owner excluded, owner
offstage) leave one orphan for as long as the bubble shows (a keyboard switch, `Alt+2`, with the
mouse resting on a tooltip). Fix: `Tooltip.dismissAllToolTips()` in the shell's `_setMode` when
the mode changes; a probe shows the bubble is gone in the same frame, with no orphan.
- **an autocomplete list under a field that also has a tooltip.** `RawAutocomplete` is an overlay
portal too; an open option list under a `Tooltip` around the field leaves an orphan. An
autocomplete alone is fine. The rev picker (`lib/ui/pr_view.dart`) has no tooltip around the
field (its `ClearButton` has one inside it), and its test passes; a tooltip added around a picker
would bring this case in.
- not a problem: a list scrolled so that a row with a shown tooltip leaves the view (the row is
disposed with its bubble, or the bubble keeps a parent); `PopupMenuButton` and `showMenu` open a
route, not an overlay portal.
## Technical notes
- `test/support/tooltip_semantics.dart`: `expectTooltipsInSemantics(tester)` shows each
on-screen `Tooltip` with `TooltipState.ensureTooltipVisible`, pumps, checks
`orphanOverlayNodes(tester)`, and dismisses it again (`Tooltip.dismissAllToolTips`).
- `orphanOverlayNodes` collects the nodes with a `traversalChildIdentifier` from the hit-test
children (`visitChildren`) and the nodes reachable through
`debugListChildrenInOrder(DebugSemanticsDumpOrder.traversalOrder)`; the difference is the orphans.
- The bubble node has no label of its own (the message is the owner's `tooltip` property), so a
test can't look for the bubble by its text.
- An upstream Flutter issue is worth filing: a merge could keep all the identifiers, or the bubble
could fall back to its hit-test parent.
- CLAUDE.md gets the cause and the fix next to the note about error 144.
# Tasks
## 1. Find the cause
- [x] 1.1 read the semantics tree of the running app over the VM service (node 2495 is gone by then;
the id is the next free one, not a place)
- [x] 1.2 trace the overlay portal semantics in Flutter: only the first `traversalParentIdentifier`
survives a merge
- [x] 1.3 reproduce in a widget test: the second tooltip in one tappable node leaves an orphan, a
`Semantics(container: true)` around it fixes it
## 2. Test helper (in progress)
- [x] 2.1 `test/support/tooltip_semantics.dart`: show every tooltip, fail on orphan overlay nodes
(found by `traversalChildIdentifier`; the bubble node has no label)
- [x] 2.2 call it from the view tests that show tooltips: Add and Ignore, Repos, Ignore dialog and
pane, Settings, Log, rev picker, status bar, preview pane, merge actions, commit message, Tasks
- [ ] 2.3 cover the rest: Directories, network dialog, checkout dialog, Help (place the call where
tooltips are on screen), Pull request and Changes with data
- [x] 2.4 fix `_SideTab` in Add and Ignore (`Semantics(container: true)`), so its test passes
## 3. Look for similar problems
- [x] 3.1 other overlay portals: an open `RawAutocomplete` under a field with a `Tooltip` leaves an
orphan; the rev picker doesn't do that today; `PopupMenuButton` and `showMenu` are routes
- [x] 3.2 other ways to orphan a bubble: a mode switch while a tooltip shows (owner excluded or
offstage) leaves one; a list scrolling the row away does not
- [x] 3.3 findings recorded in the proposal
- [x] 3.4 fix the mode switch: `Tooltip.dismissAllToolTips()` in the shell's `_setMode` when the
mode changes; the shell test checks that the bubble is gone after `Alt+1` (in the full shell the
left-behind bubble kept a parent, so the test can't check for an orphan there; the minimal probe

## 4. Wrap up

# tooltips clear of a large mouse pointer
Tags: ops, ui, accessibility
Status: Proposed, for TASK-210. Not started.
## Why
Windows lets the mouse pointer be made much bigger (Settings > Accessibility > Mouse pointer and
touch, size 1 to 15). With a pointer about four times the usual size, the app's tooltips appear
right under it and are hidden by it: the explanation is there but cannot be read.
## The idea
- The app knows how big the pointer is and places every tooltip below the pointer's reach, so the
whole tooltip shows under the arrow.
- It follows a change: making the pointer bigger or smaller in Windows moves the tooltips on the
next one shown, without a restart.
- A setting in Settings for when the detection is wrong or not wanted: **Tooltip distance**,
`Automatic` (from the pointer size) or a fixed distance.
## Use cases
- My pointer is at size 6. I rest it on the rail's Changes icon. The tooltip appears under the tip
of the arrow, below its body, and I can read it.
- I set the pointer back to size 1. The tooltips sit close to their items again, as before.
- Automatic guesses wrong on my machine. In Settings I set the distance by hand.
## Technical
- Where Windows keeps the size
- `HKCU\Control Panel\Cursors\CursorBaseSize` (DWORD, pixels: 32 by default, up to 256), which
the accessibility size slider writes; `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Accessibility\CursorSize` (1-15)
is the slider's step
- `GetSystemMetrics(SM_CYCURSOR)` gives the nominal cursor size, but on recent Windows it does not
always follow the accessibility size: the registry value is the one to trust, checked on a real
machine first
- read it in the runner (`windows/runner`, C++, `RegGetValueW`) and hand it to Dart over a method
channel, or from Dart with `win32` FFI; the runner also sees `WM_SETTINGCHANGE` (sent when the
pointer size changes) and tells Dart to read it again
- Placing the tooltips
- Flutter places a tooltip relative to its widget, not the pointer: `verticalOffset` from the
widget's centre (24 by default), `preferBelow`. One app-wide value in the theme
(`TooltipThemeData.verticalOffset`) moves them all
- the distance: the pointer's height in logical pixels (`CursorBaseSize / devicePixelRatio`,
the arrow's hot spot is its top-left) minus the half height of a small target, at least the
default 24; a widget that sets its own `verticalOffset` adds to it rather than overrides it
- a tooltip near the bottom of the window flips above (Flutter does this already when there is
no room below)
- The setting
- `Prefs`: `tooltipDistance` (`auto` or a number); Settings gets a row with Automatic and a number
field, showing what Automatic found ("pointer 128 px → 64 px")
- off Windows (macOS, Linux) Automatic is the default 24
- Tests: the theme's offset follows a given pointer size; the setting overrides it; a fake
settings-change message makes the next tooltip use the new size
# Tasks
- [ ] 1 on a real machine: which value follows the accessibility pointer size (`CursorBaseSize`,
`CursorSize`, `SM_CYCURSOR`), at sizes 1, 6 and 15
- [ ] 2 read it in the runner, hand it to Dart; read it again on `WM_SETTINGCHANGE`
- [ ] 3 `TooltipThemeData.verticalOffset` from the pointer size, app-wide
- [ ] 4 Settings: Tooltip distance, Automatic or a number; shows what Automatic found
- [ ] 5 tests; `PLAN.md` (Settings)
# undo a discard, instead of asking first
Status: Open proposal, not decided, not to be implemented yet. There is no backlog task yet; one gets
made if we go ahead.
## Why
In the Changes mode, discarding a file or a hunk asks "Discard changes? This can't be undone." every
time. I know what the discard button does. I pressed it because I want that hunk gone, and the
question only slows me down. When I clean up a file with six hunks I do not want six dialogs. I want
to click, see the hunk disappear, and go on.
The question is there for a good reason: a discard really is permanent today. Git has no copy of an
unstaged edit, so once Ops throws it away, it is gone. That is why the dialog exists, and it is why
simply deleting the dialog would be a bad trade. I would be one mis-click away from losing an hour
of work with no way back.
So the proposal swaps the question for a safety net. Ops stops asking and starts remembering. Every
file or hunk that gets discarded is first copied into a small collection that lives as long as the
app runs. Later, in the UI, I can look through what I discarded and put any of it back. The
discard becomes cheap to do and cheap to take back, which is what I actually want from a button
like this, instead of an expensive one that has to be guarded.
## The idea
A state object for the running session, the discard bin, that collects everything discarded:
- when I discard a hunk or a file, Ops first records what is about to be lost, as a patch (the same
text `git apply` reads), together with when, which file, how many lines went, and a short preview
- then the discard runs, with no confirmation
- the recorded patches can be reapplied later from the UI, which puts the lines back into the work
tree as unstaged changes, exactly where a discard took them from
Two rules shape how it behaves.
**It is kept per project and per branch.** A patch made against one branch's version of a file
usually does not apply to another branch's version, so a flat list of everything would mostly
offer things that cannot be put back. Each entry is filed under the project (the repository) and the
branch that was checked out when I discarded it. The Changes mode shows the entries of the project
and branch I am looking at; switching branch shows that branch's entries.
**It only lives for the session.** The bin is memory, not a file. When I close Ops, it is empty
again. That is on purpose: it is a short-term safety net for "oops, not that one", not an archive,
and nothing gets written to disk that I would later have to clean up or that could leak.
## Use cases
Each case is written from where I sit: what I do, what I see, and which part of the idea handles it.
The project is `webshop`. The main checkout is on `feature/cms-updates`, and `main` is another
branch of the same project.
### Cleaning up a file with several hunks
I have debug prints in `lib/cart.dart`, in six places, and I want them all gone. In the Changes mode
I select the file and click discard on the first hunk. The hunk disappears at once, with no dialog,
and I do the same for the other five.
I see each hunk vanish as I click. Behind the scenes, six entries were added to the bin for
`webshop` / `feature/cms-updates`. Nothing in the flow asked me anything.
### I discarded the wrong hunk
On the fourth click I notice that the hunk I just threw away was a real fix, not a debug print. I
open the discarded list in the Changes mode, find the newest entry for `lib/cart.dart`, with its
preview showing the lines, and press reapply. The lines are back in the work tree, unstaged,
at the place they came from, and the entry leaves the list (or is marked as reapplied).
This case needs the list to be easy to reach and to show enough of each entry that I can recognize it
at a glance: the file, the time, and the changed lines.
### I discarded a whole file's changes
I click discard on `config/dev.yaml`, meaning to drop my local tweak. A minute later I remember that
the tweak held a value I still needed. The bin has one entry for the file with all its hunks
together. I reapply it, and the file has my tweak again.
An untracked file is the harder variant: discarding it deletes the file. For this to be undoable,
the entry has to keep the whole content of the file, not just a diff. That is still small for text
files, and is one of the open questions below for large or binary ones.
### Switching branches
I discard a hunk on `feature/cms-updates`, then switch to `main` to look at something. The
discarded list now shows `main`'s entries, which are empty, so I do not see an entry that would not
apply here anyway. When I switch back to `feature/cms-updates`, the entry is there again.
### The file changed since the discard
I discarded a hunk in `lib/cart.dart`, then edited the file further, and now the old lines do not
fit where they were. I press reapply. Git's patch apply tolerates small shifts in line numbers, so
if the surroundings are still recognizable, the hunk goes back in at its new position. If not, Ops
says the patch no longer applies, the entry stays in the list, and the file is not touched. I can
still see the preview and copy the lines out by hand.
### I close the app
I quit Ops at the end of the day. The next day the bin is empty. Anything I discarded yesterday and
did not reapply is gone, as it is today. Nothing was written to disk.
## How it works
### Where the patch comes from
The backend already builds the patch for a hunk when it discards one (`hunk_patch` in
`git.lua`, applied in reverse). The simplest, safest capture is to let the backend return that patch
from `discard_hunk`, so the copy and the discard are the same step and cannot drift apart. For a
whole file, `discard` would return the unstaged diff of the file (`git diff -- path`) before it runs
`git restore`; for an untracked file it would return the file's content, since the discard deletes
it.
The frontend then files what came back under the project and the branch:
- **project**: the repository root, which the session already knows (`RepoInfo.root`)
- **branch**: the current branch name at the moment of the discard; on a detached HEAD, the short
commit id, so a detached session still has a key
### The state object
A `ChangeNotifier` under `lib/state/`, like the other state objects, so tests can drive it without
widgets:
- an entry holds: an id, the time, project, branch, the file path, whether it was a hunk, a whole
file, or a deleted untracked file, the patch text, and the counts of added and removed lines
- `record(entry)` is called by the Changes state right before the discard goes to the backend
- `entriesFor(project, branch)` is what the UI lists, newest first
- `reapply(entry)` asks the backend to apply the patch to the work tree (not to the index), and on
success drops the entry
- it is created with the session and dropped with it, never saved
The Changes state's `discardFile` and `discardHunk` call it, and `confirmDiscard` disappears from
those two paths. The shared `ConfirmDialog` stays; the merge and archive questions keep using it.
### Reapplying
The backend gets a call that applies a stored patch to the work tree, with `git apply`, not
`--cached`, so the lines come back as unstaged changes, as before. The same checks a discard
already has apply: a file with unsaved changes in Neovim is refused, so Ops never writes under a
buffer that has newer text. A patch that no longer applies is reported with git's own message, and
the entry stays. For a deleted untracked file the call writes the stored content back, and refuses
if a file now exists at that path.
### Where it shows up in the UI
Not decided. The candidates, from least to most room:
- **A note with Undo, right after the discard.** Ops already has a short note with an Undo button
that stays 3 seconds, or while the mouse is over it. It fits "oops, not that one" with no
navigation at all. It is not enough alone, because it is gone after a few seconds, but it
covers the most common case for free.
- **A "Discarded" button in the Changes header, with a count.** It opens a popover or a panel with
the list for this project and branch. Small, always in the same place, and empty most of the
time.
- **A third list in the Changes mode**, next to STAGED and CHANGES, shown only when the bin has
entries for this project and branch. More visible, but it takes room from the file lists and
brings its own keys and focus rules.
My lean is the first two together: the note for the immediate case, the header button for the
rest. That is still to be decided.
## Open questions
- Where the list lives (above), and whether reapply has a key. Any key is a separate decision, since
keys can conflict with the existing ones.
- How many entries to keep. Entries are small text, but a session can run for days. A cap per
project and branch (say the newest 200), or a total size cap, dropping the oldest first, would keep
memory bounded. Which one, and what number.
- Large and binary files. A discarded binary file, or a very large text file, cannot sensibly be
held as text. Options: keep the confirmation for those, and only those; or refuse to discard them
without the dialog; or store the bytes up to a limit.
- Whole-file discard of a file with both staged and unstaged parts: only the unstaged part is
discarded today, and only that part would be recorded.
- Whether a reapplied entry is removed or kept and marked, so the list shows that it was put back.
- Whether the discarded list can show other branches of the same project, with a switch, since a
patch may still apply after a branch is rebased or a hunk is cherry-picked.
- A bulk discard ("discard all", if it ever exists) should be one entry group, not hundreds.
## Impact
- `nvimos-poc-frontend`: a new state object under `lib/state/`, `ChangesState.discardFile` and
`discardHunk` record first, `confirmDiscard` removed from those two paths, a UI place for the list,
PLAN.md (Changes mode, and the "General requirements" note about confirmations)
- `nvimos-poc-backend`: `discard` and `discard_hunk` return what they removed, and a new call
applies a stored patch to the work tree
- tests: the state object (record, per project and branch, reapply, no longer applies), the backend
calls (capture, reapply, refusing a buffer with unsaved changes), and a widget test that a
discard no longer opens a dialog
- no change to the merge and archive confirmations
# Ops on the web: a demo that runs in the browser
Status: Open proposal, not decided. Draft for discussion; the open questions at the end need
answers before anything is built.
## Why
Showing Ops to someone today means they install a Windows app, clone a repo and maybe start
Neovim. That is a lot to ask from someone who only wants to see what it looks like. A link they
can open in a browser, with no install and nothing to set up, is a much easier first step.
Flutter builds for the web, and the app is already split where it needs to be: every mode talks to
git through one interface, `RepoBackend`, and the Tasks mode gets its files through it too. The
desktop app implements that interface by running `git`. A web build can implement it a second
time, as a fake repo that lives in the browser.
The web version is a demo, not a second product. It does not need to be perfect, and it never
touches a real repo. It shows the real UI, with real planning data, and lets a visitor click
through everything: stage a hunk, commit, merge a branch with conflicts, ignore a folder, tick a
box on a task. All of that is mocked: the changes are kept in the browser's storage and go nowhere
else.
## The idea
The demo is a static website: the Ops web build plus its data, served from GitHub Pages or any
other static host. There is no server.
It starts from two things baked into the site when it is built:
- a small demo repo, exported to JSON: its files, commits and branches, with one branch that
conflicts on purpose so the Merge view has something to show
- a snapshot of this project's planning (`backlog/` and `openspec/` from `nvimos/meta`), so the
Tasks mode shows the real tasks and changes
Whatever the visitor does goes into a layer on top of that starting point, saved in the browser's
`localStorage`. Reloading the page keeps it; a "Reset demo" button throws it away and starts over.
Nothing is ever written to GitHub or any other remote, and the "read-only" in the name means
exactly that: the real repos are only read, never changed.
The modes that need a real computer are left out of the web build: Neovim, the terminals, the file
manager, the external editors, "open in editor". The modes that work on a repo (Pull request,
Changes, Add and Ignore, Repos, Tasks, History, Help) all run against the fake repo.
A banner (or a mark in the status bar) says this is a demo whose changes stay in this browser, and
links to the release page for the real app.
### Taking the work out: patches
The mocked writes don't have to be thrown away. Everything the visitor did is a set of real changes
to real files: commits with messages, staged hunks, edited task files. The demo can hand them out
as patches, the same text git itself would produce, to download as a file or copy to the
clipboard. Applied in a real checkout (`git am` for commits, `git apply` for the rest), they become
real work.
That makes the web version more than a toy. Someone can open a project's planning in the browser,
tick boxes, move a task to In Progress, write a new task or fix a typo in a proposal, and send the
result as a patch or paste it into a pull request, all without cloning anything. The demo stays
read-only towards the remote; the patch is how the work leaves the browser, and the person decides
where it goes.
Later, the same build could open other repos: a visitor pastes a GitHub URL and the demo reads
that repo's planning and files instead of the baked-in ones. That is a second step and not part of
the first version; see the open questions.
## Use cases
**A link in a message.** I send Erik a link. He opens it on his work laptop, where he can't
install anything. Ops appears in the browser with the Tasks mode open: our real backlog, task 196
in To Do, the ignore panes in progress. He opens a change and reads its proposal. (The baked-in
planning snapshot.)
**Trying the git modes.** Erik switches to Changes. There are a few modified files in the demo
repo. He stages one hunk, writes a commit message and commits. The commit shows up in Pull
request's commit list. (The fake repo and its browser layer.)
**A merge with conflicts.** He picks the `feature/rename` branch and merges it. Two files
conflict; the Merge view lights up, he picks a side for each hunk and finishes the merge. (The
three-way merge in Dart, and the branch that conflicts on purpose.)
**Starting over.** Erik's colleague Nora opens the same link in the same browser the next day and
sees Erik's commit. She clicks Reset demo and gets the repo as it was. (The layer in
`localStorage`, and the reset.)
**Taking a change home.** Nora reads the planning in the browser and sees that task 142 is
already done. She ticks its last box, sets it to Done, and commits "backlog: task 142 done". Then
she clicks "Export patches" and copies them. In her real checkout of `nvimos/meta` she runs
`git am` on the copied text, and the commit is there, with her message, ready to push. (The
patch export.)
**What isn't there.** Nora looks for the Neovim connection. The web build doesn't show it; the
banner says the full app has it and links to the download. (Desktop-only parts left out.)
## Technical notes
### What the code allows today
- `lib/tasks/` uses no `dart:io`: the Tasks workspace already reads through `RepoBackend.listFiles`
and `readFiles`
- 26 files under `lib/` import `dart:io`: all of `lib/local/`, `lib/rpc/client.dart`,
`lib/main.dart`, and in the shell's path `state/session.dart`, `state/prefs.dart`,
`state/repos.dart`, `state/preview.dart`, `state/nvim_launcher.dart`, `timing/ui_timing.dart`,
`ui/preview_pane.dart` and a few more
- `RepoBackend` (`lib/backend/repo_backend.dart`) has 47 methods: branches, log, diff, status,
stage / unstage / discard per file and per hunk, checkout, merge, rebase, commit, the merge
steps (`mergePreflight`, `mergeStart`, `mergeHunks`, `mergePick`, `mergeFinish`, `mergeAbort`),
`listFiles`, `readFiles`, `setLines`, `move`, and more
- the local backend runs `git` and parses its output (`lib/local/local_backend.dart`,
`diff_parse.dart`, `git_repo.dart`); Add and Ignore uses `git check-ignore -v`
- the `git` package in `pubspec.yaml` runs processes and must not be imported by the web build
### The web entry point
- `lib/main_web.dart`, built with `flutter build web -t lib/main_web.dart`
- it never imports `lib/local/` or `lib/rpc/`; a test (or an analyzer rule) checks that nothing in
its import graph pulls in `dart:io`
- the shell parts that touch `dart:io` get web-safe versions behind conditional imports
(`if (dart.library.js_interop)`): prefs in `localStorage`, `UiTiming` without files, a session
that has no Neovim
- the mode list is filtered: modes that only make sense on a desktop are not shown
- PDF stays off (it is off by default already)
### The fake repo (`DemoBackend`)
- implements `RepoBackend` in plain Dart, so it also runs on the desktop and in tests
- the repo state: a map of files for HEAD, the index and the working tree; commits are snapshots
(a parent, a message, an author, a time, the file map); branches are names pointing at commits
- status: compare working tree with index, index with HEAD
- diffs: a line diff (Myers) gives the hunks; staging a hunk applies it to the index, discarding
it applies it backwards to the working tree
- log and checkout follow commit parents and swap the file maps
- merge: a line-based three-way merge (diff3) against the common ancestor; overlapping changes
become conflicts in the `ConflictHunk` shape the Merge view already reads
- rebase: replay commits one by one with the same merge, or leave it out at first
- Add and Ignore: `.gitignore` matching in Dart (a pub package if a good one exists, else about 150
lines), returning what `git check-ignore -v` returns: the file, the rule, its line
- `setLines` and `move` change the working tree, so task edits and file renames work
- the layer: every change is a small event or a new state saved under one key in `localStorage`
(JSON); the starting point comes from the baked-in JSON; Reset deletes the key
- `localStorage` holds about 5 MB per site; the demo repo must stay well under it, or the layer
moves to IndexedDB
### Patch export
- commits made in the demo: one `git format-patch` style mail per commit (`From`, `Subject`,
`Date`, the message, the unified diff), all in one mbox text, so `git am` takes them in order
- uncommitted changes: a plain unified diff (`diff --git a/... b/...`) of index and working tree
against HEAD, for `git apply` (staged and unstaged as one patch, or two; to decide)
- the diffs come from the same line diff the views use; headers carry the file modes and the
`index <old>..<new>` blob ids only if the fake computes real git blob hashes (SHA-1 of
`blob <size>\0<content>`), else they are left out, which `git apply` accepts
- the base commit is named (`base-commit:` trailer), so the receiver knows where the patches fit;
with a baked-in snapshot that is the real commit sha it was taken from
- Download (a `.patch` / `.mbox` file through a browser download) and Copy (the clipboard API)
- for a real repo opened by URL the patches apply to that repo; for the made-up demo repo they are
only a demonstration
- line endings and a missing newline at the end of a file must come out exactly as git writes
them, or `git apply` refuses; tests apply the exported patches with real git
### Baking the data
- a tool (`tool/demo_export.dart`, run in CI) exports a real git repo to the JSON the fake reads:
the commits of chosen branches, their file maps (deduplicated by content hash), the authors
- the planning snapshot: `backlog/` and `openspec/` from `nvimos/meta` `main`, the same files the
`tracking-remote-snapshot` change fetches, stored as the tracking folder of the demo repo
- both are assets of the web build, loaded at start
### Hosting
- static files only: `index.html`, `main.dart.js` or the wasm build, the renderer, the assets
- GitHub Pages is enough: build with `--base-href /<repo>/` when served from a subpath; use hash
URLs so no 404 routing is needed
- GitHub Pages can't set response headers; the multithreaded wasm renderer needs COOP/COEP, so it
runs single-threaded there. Cloudflare Pages or Netlify can set the headers if that matters
- first load is about 2 to 3 MB for the renderer and the app, plus the data
- a GitHub Action builds and publishes on every push to `main` of ops, and on a push to
`nvimos/meta` (or nightly) for fresh planning
### Tests
- `DemoBackend` gets unit tests per operation, the same way the local backend has them
- the existing widget tests could run against `DemoBackend` instead of real git where they only
need a repo; that would make them faster and keep them inside the fake clock
- one smoke test builds the web target in CI
## Relation to other changes
- `tracking-remote-snapshot`: same planning data, same read-only view of a remote repo; the web
demo bakes in what the desktop app would fetch
- `purrage-backend-seam` and `purrage-local-git-backend`: the backend seam the fake plugs into
- `bootstrap-and-ci`: the CI the web build and its publishing go into
## Open questions
1. **Read-only or mocked writes?** The name says read-only; the plan above mocks every write in
the browser. Is "read-only" about the real repos only, or should the first version really be
read-only (Tasks and diffs to look at, no stage, commit or merge) and the mocked writes come
second?
2. **Which repo is the demo repo?** ops itself (big, real history, real meta), a slice of it, or a
small made-up repo with a story (a few commits, a feature branch, a conflict)? A made-up one is
predictable and small; ops itself is more convincing.
3. **Whose planning?** This project's real `nvimos/meta`, or a made-up backlog that matches the
demo repo? The real one shows real work but has nothing to do with a made-up demo repo.
4. **Any GitHub URL, when?** Should a visitor be able to paste a GitHub URL in the first version?
Reading a repo from the browser: one GitHub API call
(`/repos/<o>/<r>/git/trees/<ref>?recursive=1`) lists the files, each file comes from
`raw.githubusercontent.com`; both allow requests from other sites. The zip download
(`codeload.github.com`) probably doesn't. Without a login the API allows 60 calls an hour per
visitor. Git history (commits, branches) for the git modes would need many more calls; is the
URL feature Tasks-only?
5. **Other git hosts.** A browser can't speak the git protocol to an arbitrary server without a
CORS proxy (what isomorphic-git uses). That means running a server. Later, or never?
6. **Dart fake or isomorphic-git?** The plan uses a fake written in Dart (deterministic, no
JavaScript bridge, doubles as a test fake). isomorphic-git would be real git in the browser,
but has no `check-ignore -v`, limited conflict handling, and needs its own adapter to our
models anyway. Agreed on Dart?
7. **How much of git is faked?** Rebase, stash, discard of untracked files, renames: which are in
the first version, and which buttons are hidden or show "not in the demo"?
8. **Which modes are in?** Pull request, Changes, Add and Ignore, Repos, Tasks, History, Help seem
to fit. Does Repos make sense with one demo repo, or should the demo ship two or three repos?
9. **localStorage or sessionStorage?** localStorage keeps a visitor's work across reloads and
visits; sessionStorage forgets it when the tab closes, so every visit starts clean. Which is the
better demo? Should the layer have a version, so a new site build drops an old layer that no
longer fits the new starting point?
10. **Where is it hosted, and under what address?** GitHub Pages of `nvimos/ops`
(`nvimos.github.io/ops`), a separate `nvimos/demo` repo, or an own domain? Wasm or the JS
build?
11. **Is the web entry point worth the shell changes?** The conditional imports touch session,
prefs and timing. Is that acceptable in the main code, or should the web shell be a separate
thin app that reuses the views?
12. **Banner and links.** What does the demo banner say, and where does it link (releases page,
README, a landing page)?
13. **Analytics.** Do we want to know how many people open the demo? GitHub Pages has none; adding
a tracker brings a cookie banner. Probably no.
14. **Keys in the browser.** Some app-wide keys (Alt+1..9, Ctrl+B) may be taken by the browser.
Which ones collide, and do they need web alternatives?
15. **Size of the work.** Rough guess: one to two weeks, most of it the three-way merge and the
ignore matching. Is that worth it now, or after the release and CI work?
16. **Git in Dart is a project of its own.** A fake that covers status, hunks, commits, merge and
ignore rules is a small git. Can the first version be much smaller: Tasks edits and file edits
only, with diffs against the snapshot and patch export, and no branches, merge or rebase? The
git modes would then come later, or show the baked-in history read-only.
17. **Patches as the way out.** Is export (download, clipboard) enough, or should the demo also
offer to open a pull request on GitHub with the patches (needs a login, so a token or an OAuth
app, and then it is no longer a static site without secrets)? Commit author: ask the visitor
for a name and email once, or leave a placeholder for `git am` to keep?
18. **Patches against a changing remote.** The snapshot is from a commit that may be old by the
time the patch is applied. Is the `base-commit:` trailer enough, or should the demo warn when
the snapshot is older than the remote's `main`?
